<code> [GTI]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The GTI object is returned.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

Here's a table of cars, each with a sentence about its engine under it, made from columns
that the table hides.

```{python}
from great_tables import GTI, md
from great_tables.data import gtcars

cars = gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "trim", "hp", "hp_rpm", "trq", "msrp"]].head(10)


def engine(row):
    return md(
        f"The **{row['trim']}** makes {row['hp']:.0f} hp at {row['hp_rpm']:,.0f} rpm, "
        f"and {row['trq']:.0f} lb-ft of torque."
    )


(
    GTI(cars, rowname_col="model")
    .cols_hide(columns=["trim", "hp", "hp_rpm", "trq"])
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_row_details(engine)
)
```

A row's details can be a table of their own. Here, each of Ontario's ten largest
municipalities has a table of its population at each census.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT
from great_tables.data import towny

years = [1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, 2016, 2021]
counts = [f"population_{year}" for year in years]
largest = towny.nlargest(10, "population_2021")[["name", "status", *counts]]


def populations(row):
    census = pd.DataFrame({"census": years, "population": [row[c] for c in counts]})
    return (
        GT(census)
        .cols_label(census="Census", population="Population")
        .fmt_integer(columns="population")
    )


(
    GTI(largest, rowname_col="name")
    .cols_hide(columns=counts[:-1])
    .fmt_integer(columns="population_2021")
    .i_row_details(populations)
)
```

i_link(self, group: str | None, on: str | None = None) -> Self

Link the table to others on the page, so that the rows selected in one filter the others.

::: {.doc-text}

Tables with the same `group=` are linked by their `on=` column, which each of them has in
its data (it can be a hidden one). When a reader selects rows in one of them (which
[`i_selection()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_selection`) lets them do), each of the others
shows only its rows whose value in that column is one of the selected rows' values;
clearing the selection shows them all again. A row with a missing value in the column
isn't linked to any. A table whose rows can't be selected is only filtered, and tables
whose rows can be filter each other (but not themselves). The tables link in the browser,
without a server: in a Quarto document, a notebook (but not across the frames some show
each cell's output in, as Colab does), or an HTML page with the tables in it.

A table filtered by another's selection says so in its control bar, with a token
("Selected in Makes: Ferrari, Lamborghini") that shows the rows again (until the
selection changes), and in its info panel. The tables are named after their titles (see
[`tab_header()`](`great_tables.GT.tab_header`)), or else their IDs. The filter is on top
of the table's own search and filters, and isn't part of its view: it isn't kept with the
view (see [`i_view_state()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_view_state`)), undone, or in the code
an export copies.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[group]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The name of the tables' group: tables with the same one are linked. With `None`, the
    table isn't linked.

<code>[on]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The column of the table's data whose values link its rows to those of the others in
    the group (each of which has a column of that name).
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [GTI]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The GTI object is returned.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

Here are two tables of cars, one of their makes and one of the cars themselves, linked
by the make. Select some makes in the first, and the second shows only their cars.

```{python}
from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import gtcars

cars = gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
makes = cars.groupby("mfr", as_index=False).agg(models=("model", "count"))

(
    GTI(makes, rowname_col="mfr")
    .tab_header(title="Makes")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_link("cars", on="mfr")
)
```

```{python}
(
    GTI(cars, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="Cars")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_link("cars", on="mfr")
)
```


## Interactive tables in Python and apps

An interactive table's view (its search, filters and sort) and selection can be read and set from Python: in a notebook, with the table as a widget, and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara apps. A table with many rows can keep them in Python and send the browser a page at a time. Pages an app makes itself (with Flask, Django or FastHTML) can show the tables, with their runtime once.



i_as_widget(self) -> GTIWidget

Show the table as a widget, whose view and selection can be read and set from Python.

::: {.doc-text}

The widget (an [anywidget](https://anywidget.dev)) shows the table as it's shown anywhere
else, in a notebook in Jupyter, VS Code or Colab, or in marimo (where
[`mo_gti()`](`great_tables.marimo.mo_gti`) shows it as a UI element, so that the cells
that read it run again with each change), and keeps Python up to date with what the
reader does with it: the rows its search and filters keep, in the order shown, and those
selected. Python can change the table's filters, sort, search and selection, too, and the
table shows the change. The table works in the browser, as without a widget: Python is
told what it does.

The widget has these, to read and set:

- `query`: the filters, as a query in text (as the query box has it, e.g.
  `'category in ("Tools") and margin > 0.2'`), or `""` without any; set it to a query (in
  text, or as [`i_view()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_view`)'s `filter=` takes it), or to `""`.
- `search`: the search, or `""`.
- `sort`: the columns the rows are sorted by, most significant first, with a `-` before
  each one sorted in descending order (e.g., `["-net", "store"]`).
- `selection`: the data rows selected (numbered by position in the data, from 0), in data
  order, as far as [`i_selection()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_selection`) lets readers select
  them.

And these, to read:

- `rows`: the data rows the search and filters keep (and linked tables' selections; see
  [`i_link()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_link`)), in the order shown, on every page.
- `view()`: the table's data with those rows, as a DataFrame of the data's library (with
  all its columns); `view(selected=True)` has the rows selected.

And `on_change(callback)` has `callback` called, with the widget, after each change the
reader makes (`on_change(callback, remove=True)` stops it).

The rows are the browser's: a change made from Python is applied by the browser once the
code making it has run, so in a notebook, `rows` and `view()` have it in the next cell (in
the same cell, they raise an error). Before the widget is shown, they're those of the
table's view (see [`i_view()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_view`)), as Python finds them.

A table with more rows than the browser is quick with keeps them in Python instead (see
[`i_scale()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_scale`)), which sends the browser a page at a time:
then the rows are Python's, and `rows` and `view()` have a change at once.

The widget needs the `anywidget` package (`pip install anywidget`, or
`pip install great_tables[widget]`).
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [GTIWidget]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The widget, which shows the table when it's a cell's output (or with `display()`).
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

Here the reader can filter the cars by their make and select some; Python gets them.

```python
from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import gtcars

cars = gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]

widget = (
    GTI(cars, rowname_col="model")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_as_widget()
)
widget
```

In a later cell, after filtering and selecting:

```python
widget.query           # 'mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")'
widget.view()          # those makes' cars, as a Pandas DataFrame
widget.view(selected=True)
```

And from Python, the table shows the cars with the most power first:

```python
widget.sort = "-hp"
```

i_scale(self, engine: Engine = 'auto', rows: RowsMode = 'inline') -> Self

Set where the rows of the table are searched, filtered and sorted (shown as a widget or in a Shiny app), and where a large table's rows are kept (written as a page).

::: {.doc-text}

A table shown in the browser has all of its rows there, which does all of this: quick for
a table of a few thousand rows, but slow to load (and to sort) with many more. Shown as a
widget (with [`i_as_widget()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_as_widget`)), or in a Shiny app (with
[`render_gt()`](`great_tables.shiny.render_gt`)), a table can keep its rows in Python
instead (in the notebook's kernel, or on the app's server), which searches, filters and
sorts them (with [Narwhals](https://narwhals-dev.github.io/narwhals/), on the data's own
library), and sends the browser the page it shows, one at a time: so the table loads as
quickly with a million rows as with a few.

In the kernel, a table always has pages (as [`i_pagination()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_pagination`)
sets them up), and its readers can't group its rows by a column, see its columns'
profiles, see rows' details, or export the rows themselves (they can copy the code that
filters and sorts the data as the view does, if the table has the `"code"` format); nor
do its `data_color()` colors change with the rows kept, or does it filter linked tables
(see [`i_link()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_link`)). A table with row groups, summary rows, or a
stub of more than one column is shown in the browser, as anywhere else, and so is a table
that isn't shown as a widget or in a Shiny app.

A table of a lazy frame (a Polars LazyFrame, a DuckDB relation or an Ibis table) keeps its
rows in the frame, and has only the page shown collected (see [`GTI()`](`great_tables.GTI`)).

In the browser, a table of pages with more than 3,000 rows has the rows past its first page
in its HTML as data, which the browser makes into rows as they're shown. With
`rows="asset"`, [`write_raw_html()`](`great_tables.GT.write_raw_html`) writes them to a
file of their own beside the page instead (`page.gti.json`, for `page.html`), which the
table fetches as it loads: the page is smaller, and quicker to load, and the browser keeps
the file for the next visit, but the page needs the file beside it, served with it (a page
opened from a file can't fetch it, in most browsers). Shown anywhere else (in a notebook,
a Quarto document, or with `as_raw_html()`), the table has its rows in its HTML. Until the
file has come, the table shows its first page, and the search, filters and sorting wait for
it; if it doesn't come, the table has only its first page.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[engine]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Engine]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;auto&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Where the rows are searched, filtered and sorted: in Python, if the table is shown as a
    widget or in a Shiny app and has more rows than the browser is quick with (more than
    3,000, or more than 10 MB of HTML), and in the browser otherwise (`"auto"`, the
    default); in the browser (`"browser"`); or in Python, if the table is shown as a widget
    or in a Shiny app (`"kernel"`).

<code>[rows]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [RowsMode]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;inline&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Where a large table's rows past its first page are, written as a page with
    `write_raw_html()`: in its HTML (`"inline"`, the default), or in a file beside it
    (`"asset"`).
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [GTI]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The GTI object is returned.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

This table of a million rows is shown a page at a time, from Python.

```python
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GTI

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
df = pl.DataFrame({"x": rng.normal(size=1_000_000), "n": rng.integers(0, 100, 1_000_000)})

GTI(df).fmt_number(columns="x").i_cols_filter().i_scale(engine="kernel").i_as_widget()
```

This page of the `sp500` dataset has the rows past its first page in `sp500.gti.json`,
beside it.

```python
from great_tables import GTI
from great_tables.data import sp500

GTI(sp500).i_pagination().i_scale(rows="asset").write_raw_html("sp500.html", make_page=True)
```

render_gt() -> GtTransformer.OutputRendererDecorator
render_gt(_fn: GtTransformer.ValueFn) -> GtTransformer.OutputRenderer

Render a great_tables table.

::: {.doc-text}

An interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) gives the app
its state as inputs, for an output with id `id`:

- `input.<id>_view()`: the table's view, a dict with its filters as a query in text
  (`"query"`), its `"search"`, its `"sort"` (columns, with a `-` before those in descending
  order), its `"page"` and `"page_size"`, its `"hidden"` columns and the column its rows are
  grouped by (`"group_by"`);
- `input.<id>_rows()`: the data rows its search and filters keep (and linked tables'
  selections), in the order shown, on every page, numbered by position in the data (from 0);
- `input.<id>_selection()`: the data rows selected, in data order.

They're set once the table is shown, then after each change to them, whether the reader
makes it or the server does, with [`update_gti()`](`great_tables.shiny.update_gti`). A table
rendered again starts again with the view it's given.

A `GTI` table with more rows than the browser is quick with keeps them on the server instead
(see [`i_scale()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_scale`)), which sends the browser a page at a time:
then `input.<id>_rows()` is found on the server, from the table's view (without linked
tables' selections).
:::

output_gt(id: str, placeholder: bool | None = None) -> Tag

Output UI for a great_tables table.

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[id]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   An output id.

<code>[placeholder]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Deprecated and has no effect. This argument was never implemented and will be removed in a
    future release.
:::

update_gti(id: str, *, query: str | dict[str, Any] | None = None, search: str | None = None, sort: str | list[str] | None = None, selection: list[int] | None = None, session: Session | None = None) -> None

Change an interactive table's view or selection, from a Shiny app's server.

::: {.doc-text}

The table (rendered with [`render_gt()`](`great_tables.shiny.render_gt`)) is filtered,
searched, sorted, and has its rows selected, as if the reader had done it (so that a change to
its filters, search or sort shows its first page). What isn't given (or is `None`) is left as
it is. The table's inputs then give the new state (see `render_gt()`).
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[id]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table's output id.

<code>[query]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | dict[str, Any] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The table's filters: a query in text (as the query box has it), or as
    [`i_view()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_view`)'s `filter=` takes it; `""` for none.

<code>[search]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The table's search; `""` for none.

<code>[sort]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | list[str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The columns to sort the table by, most significant first, each with a `-` before it to
    sort it in descending order (e.g., `["-net", "store"]`), or one column; `[]` to leave it
    unsorted.

<code>[selection]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The data rows to select (numbered by position in the data, from 0), and only those; `[]`
    for none. The table must let readers select rows (with
    [`i_selection()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_selection`)).

<code>[session]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Session | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The Shiny session (by default, the current one).
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```python
from shiny import App, reactive, render, ui
from great_tables import GTI, exibble
from great_tables.shiny import output_gt, render_gt, update_gti

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_action_button("big", "Largest first"),
    output_gt("table"),
    ui.output_text("shown"),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render_gt
    def table():
        return GTI(exibble).i_cols_filter(columns="fctr", type="facet")

    @render.text
    def shown():
        return f"{len(input.table_rows())} rows, filtered by {input.table_view()['query']!r}"

    @reactive.effect
    @reactive.event(input.big)
    def _():
        update_gti("table", query='fctr in ("one", "two")', sort="-num")


app = App(app_ui, server)
```

st_gti(table: GT, *, key: str, on_change: Literal['rerun', 'ignore'] | Callable[[], Any] = 'rerun') -> GTIState

Show an interactive table in a Streamlit app, and get its state.

::: {.doc-text}

The table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) is shown as a component,
and its state is given back: its view, the rows the view keeps, and those selected (see
[`GTIState`](`great_tables.streamlit.GTIState`)). Each change the reader makes to them (a
search, a filter, a sort, a selection, ...) runs the app again, and the table's state is then
what the reader made it. [`update_gti()`](`great_tables.streamlit.update_gti`) changes it
from the app.

A `GTI` table with more rows than the browser is quick with keeps them in Python instead (see
[`i_scale()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_scale`)), and sends the browser a page at a time: the
browser asks for each one (and for a filter's counts) by running the app again, which answers.
Then the rows its view keeps are found in Python (without linked tables' selections). Such a
table is best made once, with `st.cache_resource`: a table the app makes again on each run is
rendered again each time (which, with many rows in a DataFrame, takes a while).
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[table]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [GT]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table to show: a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`.

<code>[key]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table's key, unique in the app: the table keeps its view and selection by it (when
    it's made again on each run, but rendered the same), and `update_gti()` changes it.

<code>[on_change]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Literal[[&quot;rerun&quot;]{.st}, [&quot;ignore&quot;]{.st}] | Callable[[], Any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;rerun&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   What a change the reader makes does: run the app again (`"rerun"`, the default); not, so
    that the table's state is only what the app made it (`"ignore"`); or call a function (with
    no arguments), and run the app again. A table whose rows are in Python runs the app again
    for each page all the same.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [GTIState]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table's state: its view, the rows the view keeps, and those selected. Until it's
    shown, as it's first shown (its rows as Python finds them); once it's shown, as the
    browser last gave it.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```python
import streamlit as st
from great_tables import GTI, exibble
from great_tables.streamlit import st_gti

table = GTI(exibble).i_cols_filter(columns="fctr", type="facet").i_selection("multiple")
state = st_gti(table, key="table")

st.write(f"{len(state.rows or [])} rows, filtered by {state.query!r}")
st.dataframe(exibble.iloc[state.selection])
```

update_gti(key: str, *, query: str | dict[str, Any] | None = None, search: str | None = None, sort: str | list[str] | None = None, selection: list[int] | None = None) -> None

Change an interactive table's view or selection, from a Streamlit app.

::: {.doc-text}

The table (shown with [`st_gti()`](`great_tables.streamlit.st_gti`), with the same `key`) is
filtered, searched, sorted, and has its rows selected, as if the reader had done it (so that a
change to its filters, search or sort shows its first page). What isn't given (or is `None`)
is left as it is. It's changed by the table's next `st_gti()`: so call `update_gti()` before
it, as in a widget's callback (`on_click=` or `on_change=`), which is run before the app; one
called after it is the next run's.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[key]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table's key.

<code>[query]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | dict[str, Any] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The table's filters: a query in text (as the query box has it), or as
    [`i_view()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_view`)'s `filter=` takes it; `""` for none.

<code>[search]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The table's search; `""` for none.

<code>[sort]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | list[str] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The columns to sort the table by, most significant first, each with a `-` before it to
    sort it in descending order (e.g., `["-net", "store"]`), or one column; `[]` to leave it
    unsorted.

<code>[selection]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The data rows to select (numbered by position in the data, from 0), and only those; `[]`
    for none. The table must let readers select rows (with
    [`i_selection()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_selection`)).
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```python
import streamlit as st
from great_tables import GTI, exibble
from great_tables.streamlit import st_gti, update_gti

st.button(
    "Largest first",
    on_click=update_gti,
    args=("table",),
    kwargs={"query": 'fctr in ("one", "two")', "sort": "-num"},
)
state = st_gti(GTI(exibble).i_cols_filter(columns="fctr", type="facet"), key="table")
st.write(f"{len(state.rows or [])} rows, filtered by {state.query!r}")
```

GTIState(view: dict[str, Any], rows: list[int] | None, selection: list[int])

An interactive table's state in a Streamlit app, as [`st_gti()`](`great_tables.streamlit.st_gti`) gives it.

## Attributes {.doc-attributes}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[view]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [dict[str, Any]]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table's view: a dict with its filters as a query in text (`"query"`), its `"search"`,
    its `"sort"` (columns, with a `-` before those in descending order), its `"page"` and
    `"page_size"`, its `"hidden"` columns and the column its rows are grouped by
    (`"group_by"`).

<code>[rows]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The data rows its search and filters keep (and linked tables' selections), in the order
    shown, on every page, numbered by position in the data (from 0); or `None` until the
    browser has found them (when the app is run again).

<code>[selection]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The data rows selected, in data order.
:::

query: str

The table's filters, as a query in text (`""` without any).

search: str

The table's search (`""` without one).

sort: list[str]

The table's sort: its columns, each with a `-` before it if it's in descending order.

GTIPane(table: GT, **params: Any)

An interactive table in a Panel app or notebook, whose view and selection are parameters.

::: {.doc-text}

The table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) is shown as a Panel
component, and its state is in its parameters: `query`, `search` and `sort` (its view),
`rows` (the rows the view keeps) and `selection` (the rows selected). Each change the reader
makes to them sets them, so that they can be watched (with `pn.bind()`, `param.depends()` or
`.param.watch()`) like any other Panel parameter; and setting `query`, `search`, `sort` or
`selection` changes the table, as if the reader had.

A `GTI` table with more rows than the browser is quick with keeps them in Python instead (see
[`i_scale()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_scale`)), and sends the browser a page at a time. Then
`rows` is found in Python (without linked tables' selections).
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[table]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [GT]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table to show: a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`.

<code>[**params]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Panel's parameters of a component (e.g., `margin=`, `visible=`), and the pane's own
    `query=`, `search=`, `sort=` and `selection=`, which are set after the table's own view
    and selection (as if they were set once the pane's made), and checked as they are then.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```python
import panel as pn
from great_tables import GTI, exibble
from great_tables.panel import GTIPane

pn.extension()

table = GTIPane(
    GTI(exibble).i_cols_filter(columns="fctr", type="facet").i_selection("multiple")
)


def selected(selection):
    return exibble.iloc[selection]


pn.Column(table, pn.bind(selected, table.param.selection)).servable()
```

data(self, selected: bool = False) -> DataFrameLike

The table's data, with the rows its view keeps, in the order shown (see `rows`), or with `selected=True`, the rows selected (in data order): a DataFrame of the data's library, with all of its columns.

GTITable(table: GT, query: _Value[str] = None, search: _Value[str] = None, sort: _Value[list[str]] = None, selection: _Value[list[int]] = None, on_query: Callable[[str], None] | None = None, on_search: Callable[[str], None] | None = None, on_sort: Callable[[list[str]], None] | None = None, on_selection: Callable[[list[int]], None] | None = None, on_rows: Callable[[list[int]], None] | None = None) -> solara.Element

An interactive table in a Solara app, whose view and selection are the app's to read and set.

::: {.doc-text}

The table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) is shown as a widget (see
[`i_as_widget()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_as_widget`)), and its state is in the component's
values, as with Solara's own components: `query`, `search` and `sort` (its view), and
`selection` (the rows selected). Each can be a value with a callback (`on_query=`, ...) or a
reactive variable (`solara.reactive()`, `solara.use_reactive()`), which each change the reader
makes sets; and when the app changes it, the table changes, as if the reader had. One left as
`None` (as are all of them by default) starts as the table has it, and is then set. The rows
the view keeps are given to `on_rows=`.

A `GTI` table with more rows than the browser is quick with keeps them in Python instead (see
[`i_scale()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_scale`)), and sends the browser a page at a time. Then the
rows the view keeps are found in Python (without linked tables' selections). Such a table is
best made once (at the module's top level, or with `solara.use_memo()`): a table made again on
each render is rendered again each time (which, with many rows, takes a while), though the
reader's view is kept if it's rendered the same.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[table]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [GT]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table to show: a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`.

<code>[query]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [\_Value[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The table's filters, as a query in text (as the query box has it), or as
    [`i_view()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_view`)'s `filter=` takes it; `""` for none. It's set to
    a query in text.

<code>[search]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [\_Value[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The table's search; `""` for none.

<code>[sort]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [\_Value[list[str]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The columns the table is sorted by, most significant first, each with a `-` before it if
    it's sorted in descending order (e.g., `["-net", "store"]`); `[]` if it isn't sorted.

<code>[selection]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [\_Value[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The data rows selected (numbered by position in the data, from 0), in data order; `[]` for
    none. Setting it needs a table that lets readers select rows (see
    [`i_selection()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_selection`)).

<code>[on_query]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[[str], None] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Called with the new value, after each change to it (by the reader, or by the app).

<code>[on_search]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[[str], None] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Called with the new value, after each change to it (by the reader, or by the app).

<code>[on_sort]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[[str], None] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Called with the new value, after each change to it (by the reader, or by the app).

<code>[on_selection]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[[str], None] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Called with the new value, after each change to it (by the reader, or by the app).

<code>[on_rows]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[[list[int]], None] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Called with the data rows the table's search and filters keep (and linked tables'
    selections), in the order shown, on every page (numbered by position in the data, from 0),
    whenever they change: first when they're known (before the table is shown, if Python can
    find them; a `GT` table's, and one with a search, once the browser has).
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [solara.Element]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The table.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```python
import solara
from great_tables import GTI, exibble
from great_tables.solara import GTITable

table = GTI(exibble).i_cols_filter(columns="fctr", type="facet").i_selection("multiple")
query = solara.reactive("")
selection = solara.reactive([])


@solara.component
def Page():
    solara.Button("One and two", on_click=lambda: query.set('fctr in ("one", "two")'))
    GTITable(table, query=query, selection=selection)
    solara.DataFrame(exibble.iloc[selection.value])
```

runtime_tags(url: str | None = None, nonce: str | None = None) -> str

The tags that give a page the runtime its interactive tables need.

::: {.doc-text}

An interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table made with `opt_interactive()`) is a
`<gt-table>` element, made interactive by the runtime, its JavaScript and CSS. Its HTML (from
`as_raw_html()`, or as it's put in a template) is followed by the runtime, so that it works
anywhere; but a page showing several tables needs it only once. These tags, put in the page's
`<head>`, give it the runtime, and each table is then given without it, as
`as_raw_html(runtime="none")`.

The tags have the runtime itself, as a `<style>` and a `<script>`; or, given the `url=` the
app serves the runtime's files at (as [`write_runtime()`](`great_tables.web.write_runtime`)
writes them), they link to them, so that a browser keeps them as it does any other file, and
a page whose Content Security Policy doesn't allow inline scripts can have them (the table's
spec, in a `<script type="application/json">`, is data, which isn't run). The table's own CSS
is inline, in a `<style>` (and its styles in `style=` attributes), so the policy's
`style-src` must allow `'unsafe-inline'`.

The tags are HTML (a `str` with an `__html__()`), which a template (Jinja's, as Flask has, or
Django's) or FastHTML shows as it is. A table is put in a page as its HTML, from
`as_raw_html(runtime="none")`, marked safe (with `|safe` in a template, as below, or Django's
`mark_safe()`, or FastHTML's `NotStr()`).
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[url]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Where the app serves the runtime's files, `gti.js` and `gti.css` (e.g., `"/static/gti/"`).
    Each link has the file's version (`?v=`), so that a browser doesn't keep an old one. By
    default (`None`), the tags have the runtime itself.

<code>[nonce]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A nonce for the page's Content Security Policy, which the tags are given (as their
    `nonce=` attribute), so that it allows them.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The tags, as HTML (a `str` with an `__html__()`).
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

In a Flask app, with the runtime's files written to its `static/gti` folder (with
`write_runtime("static/gti")`, once), and a page with two tables:

```python
from flask import Flask, render_template_string
from great_tables import GTI, exibble
from great_tables.web import runtime_tags

app = Flask(__name__)

PAGE = (
    "<html><head>{{ runtime }}</head>"
    "<body>{{ one|safe }}{{ two|safe }}</body></html>"
)

@app.route("/")
def index():
    return render_template_string(
        PAGE,
        runtime=runtime_tags(url="/static/gti/"),
        one=GTI(exibble).as_raw_html(runtime="none"),
        two=GTI(exibble).i_selection("multiple").as_raw_html(runtime="none"),
    )
```

write_runtime(directory: str | Path) -> list[Path]

Write the runtime's files, for an app to serve.

::: {.doc-text}

The runtime that makes interactive tables interactive is two files, `gti.js` and `gti.css`,
written to `directory` (made if it isn't there) for an app to serve as static files (as a
Flask app serves its `static` folder, or Django its static files), and linked to by
[`runtime_tags(url=)`](`great_tables.web.runtime_tags`). Write them again with each new
version of Great Tables (as when the app starts, or is built), as a table needs the runtime of
its own version.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[directory]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | Path]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The directory to write the files to.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [list[Path]]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The files written.
:::


## Export

There may come a day when you need to export a table to some specific format. A great method for that is `gtsave()`, which allows us to save the table as a standalone image file or PDF. You can also get the table code as an HTML fragment with the `*_raw_html()` methods.



gtsave(self: GT, file: Path | str, selector: str = 'table', expand: int | tuple[int, int, int, int] = 5, zoom: float = 2.0, delay: float = 0.2, vwidth: int = 992, vheight: int = 744) -> GT

Save a GT table to a file (PNG, JPEG, WebP, PDF, SVG, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, RTF, or Typst).

::: {.doc-text}

The `gtsave()` method renders the table to an image or PDF using a headless Chrome browser via
the `nokap` package. This provides a reliable way to produce high-resolution image files of
tables without requiring Selenium or Playwright. Chrome or Chromium must be installed on the
system for these formats.

The other formats (SVG, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, RTF, and Typst) are written by
[gridwell](https://github.com/rich-iannone/gridwell) from the table's gridwell IR (see
`GT.as_gridwell()`), with no browser needed. Install gridwell with
`pip install "great_tables[gridwell]"`. SVG output is experimental in gridwell, and its
styling may change between gridwell releases.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[file]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Path | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The file path to write the output to. The format is determined by the file extension:
    `.png`, `.jpg`/`.jpeg`, `.webp` for images; `.pdf` for PDF; and, with gridwell, `.svg` for
    SVG, `.docx` for Word, `.xlsx` for Excel, `.pptx` for PowerPoint, `.rtf` for RTF, and
    `.typ` for Typst. If no extension is provided, `.png` is assumed. The other arguments
    apply to images and PDF only.

<code>[selector]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;table&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A CSS selector targeting the element to capture. Defaults to `"table"`, which captures just
    the table element with tight bounds.

<code>[expand]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | tuple[int, int, int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[5]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Padding (in pixels) to add around the captured element. A single integer applies equal
    padding on all sides. A 4-tuple specifies `(top, right, bottom, left)` padding individually.
    Defaults to `5`.

<code>[zoom]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The scale factor for raster image output. Higher values produce higher resolution images.
    For example, `zoom=2` produces a retina-quality (2x) image. Defaults to `2.0`. Ignored for
    PDF output.

<code>[delay]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[0.2]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Seconds to wait after page load before capturing. This is useful for ensuring that any
    web fonts or dynamic content have fully rendered. Defaults to `0.2`.

<code>[vwidth]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[992]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Viewport width in pixels. This controls the layout width of the page and may affect how the
    table is rendered (e.g., responsive layouts). Defaults to `992`.

<code>[vheight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[744]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Viewport height in pixels. Defaults to `744`.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [GT]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The GT object is returned (the same object the method is called on), facilitating method
    chaining.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

Using a small subset of the `gtcars` dataset, let's create a table and save it to a PNG file.

```python
from great_tables import GT, data
from great_tables.data import gtcars
import polars as pl

gtcars_mini = (
    data.pl.gtcars
    .select(["mfr", "model", "msrp"])
    .head(5)
)

(
    GT(gtcars_mini)
    .tab_header(title="Some Cars from gtcars")
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .gtsave("my_table.png")
)
```

Save a table as a high-resolution retina image with extra padding.

```python
(
    GT(gtcars_mini)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .gtsave("my_table.png", zoom=3, expand=20)
)
```

Save a table as a PDF.

```python
(
    GT(gtcars_mini)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .gtsave("my_table.pdf")
)
```

With gridwell installed, save the same table as SVG, or as a Word document.

```python
GT(gtcars_mini).fmt_currency(columns="msrp").gtsave("my_table.svg")
GT(gtcars_mini).fmt_currency(columns="msrp").gtsave("my_table.docx")
```

as_raw_html(self: GT, inline_css: bool = False, make_page: bool = False, all_important: bool = False, runtime: Literal['inline', 'none'] = 'inline') -> str

Get the HTML content of a GT object.

::: {.doc-text}

The `as_raw_html()` method extracts the HTML representation of a GT table and returns it as a
string. This is useful when you need to embed a table in existing HTML content, email templates,
web applications, or other contexts where you need direct access to the HTML markup rather than
displaying the table directly.

By default, the method returns an HTML fragment containing just the table and its associated
CSS styles in a `<style>` block. However, the method provides several parameters for customizing
the output format--like `inline_css=`, `make_page=`, and `all_important=`.

Body cells that have not been processed by a `fmt_*()` method are automatically HTML-escaped to
prevent cross-site scripting (XSS). Cells that have been formatted (e.g., with
[`fmt_number()`](`great_tables.GT.fmt_number`),
[`fmt_markdown()`](`great_tables.GT.fmt_markdown`), etc.) are trusted as safe HTML. To include
raw HTML in unformatted cells, use the `html()` helper (e.g., `html("<b>bold</b>")`) via a
`fmt_*()` method or `text_transform()`.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[inline_css]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   If `True`, all CSS styles are inlined into the HTML elements as `style` attributes, with
    literal values for the table's mode (`"auto"` gives the light table). Use it for email and
    for older renderers: the default `<style>` block is written with CSS custom properties,
    which email clients such as Gmail and Outlook and old engines such as wkhtmltopdf don't
    support, so they draw the table unstyled. It doesn't apply to an interactive table (one made with
    [`opt_interactive()`](`great_tables.GT.opt_interactive`)), which needs its `<style>` block
    and its script: it's ignored, with a warning (for a table in an email, use
    `opt_interactive(active=False)`).

<code>[make_page]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   If `True`, the table will be wrapped in a complete HTML page with proper `<html>`, `<head>`,
    and `<body>` tags. This is useful when you want to display the table in a web browser or
    save it as a standalone HTML file.

<code>[all_important]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   If `True`, all CSS declarations are marked with `!important` to ensure they take precedence
    over other styles that might be present in the document.

<code>[runtime]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Literal[[&quot;inline&quot;]{.st}, [&quot;none&quot;]{.st}]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;inline&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Whether an interactive table's HTML (a table made with
    [`opt_interactive()`](`great_tables.GT.opt_interactive`)) is followed by the runtime that
    makes it interactive, its JavaScript and CSS: `"inline"` (the default) or `"none"`, for a
    page that has the runtime once, however many tables it shows (see
    [`runtime_tags()`](`great_tables.web.runtime_tags`)). A static table has no runtime, so
    this doesn't change it.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   An HTML string containing the table. The format depends on the parameters passed to the
    method.
:::

## Examples: {.doc-examples}

Let's use a subset of the `gtcars` dataset to create a new table.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT, data, md, style, loc
from great_tables.data import gtcars
import polars as pl

gtcars_mini = (
    data.pl.gtcars
    .select(["mfr", "model", "msrp"])
    .head(5)
)

gt_tbl = (
    GT(gtcars_mini)
    .tab_header(
        title=md("Data listing from **gtcars**"),
        subtitle=md("gtcars is an R dataset")
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="LightCyan"),
        locations=loc.body(columns="mfr")
    )
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .tab_options(
        heading_background_color="Azure",
        table_body_hlines_color="Lavender",
        table_body_hlines_width="2px"
    )
    .opt_horizontal_padding(scale=2)
)

gt_tbl
```

Now we can return the table as an HTML string using the `as_raw_html()` method.

```{python}
gt_tbl.as_raw_html()
```

The HTML string contains the HTML for the table. It has only the table so it's not a complete
HTML document but rather an HTML fragment. While this useful for embedding a table in an
existing HTML document, you could also use the `make_page=True` argument to get a complete HTML
page with the table contained within.

```{python}
gt_tbl.as_raw_html(make_page=True)
```

Should you want to include all of the CSS styles as inline styles, you can use `inline_css=True`
to get an HTML string with all CSS inlined into the HTML tags.

```{python}
gt_tbl.as_raw_html(inline_css=True)
```

write_raw_html(gt: GT, filename: str | Path, encoding: str = 'utf-8', inline_css: bool = False, newline: str | None = None, make_page: bool = False, all_important: bool = False, runtime: Literal['inline', 'none'] = 'inline') -> None

Write the table to an HTML file.

::: {.doc-text}

This helper function saves the output of `GT.as_raw_html()` to an HTML file specified by the
user.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[gt]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [GT]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A GT object.

<code>[filename]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | Path]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   The name of the file to save the HTML. Can be a string or a `pathlib.Path` object.

<code>[encoding]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;utf-8&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The encoding used when writing the file. Defaults to 'utf-8'.

<code>[inline_css]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   An option to supply styles to table elements as inlined CSS styles. This is useful when
    including the table HTML as part of an HTML email message body, since inlined styles are
    largely supported in email clients over using CSS in a `<style>` block.

<code>[newline]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The newline character to use when writing the file. Defaults to `os.linesep`.

<code>[make_page]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   If `True`, the table is wrapped in a complete HTML page, with `<html>`, `<head>` and
    `<body>` tags.

<code>[all_important]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   If `True`, all CSS declarations are marked with `!important`.

<code>[runtime]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Literal[[&quot;inline&quot;]{.st}, [&quot;none&quot;]{.st}]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;inline&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Whether an interactive table's HTML is followed by the runtime that makes it interactive,
    its JavaScript and CSS: `"inline"` (the default) or `"none"`, for a page that has the
    runtime once, however many tables it shows (see
    [`runtime_tags()`](`great_tables.web.runtime_tags`)). A static table has no runtime, so
    this doesn't change it.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [None]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   An HTML file is written to the specified path and the method returns `None`. (A `GTI`
    table with its rows as an asset, as [`i_scale()`](`great_tables.GTI.i_scale`) sets it,
    has the rows past its first page written beside it, to a file named as the HTML file is,
    with `.gti.json` for its extension.)
:::

as_latex(self: GT, use_longtable: bool = False, tbl_pos: str | None = None) -> str

Output a GT object as LaTeX

::: {.doc-text}

The `as_latex()` method outputs a GT object as a LaTeX fragment. This method is useful for when
you need to include a table as part of a LaTeX document. The LaTeX fragment contains the table
as a string.

:::{.callout-warning}
`as_latex()` is still experimental.
:::
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[use_longtable]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   An option to use the `longtable` environment in LaTeX output. This is useful for tables that
    span multiple pages and don't require precise positioning.

<code>[tbl_pos]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The position of the table in the LaTeX output when `use_longtable=False`. Valid values for
    positioning include `"!t"` (top of page), `"!b"` (bottom of the page), `"!h"` (here),
    `"!p"` (on a separate page), and `"!H"` (exactly here). If a value is not provided then the
    table will be placed at the top of the page; if in the Quarto render then the table
    positioning option will be ignored in favor of any setting within the Quarto rendering
    environment.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A LaTeX fragment that contains the table.
:::

## Latex Packages {.doc-latex-packages}

The LaTeX fragment uses commands from these packages, which need to be loaded in the
document's preamble:

- `booktabs` (always)
- `longtable`, with `use_longtable=True`
- `hyperref`, if the table has links from [`fmt_url()`](`great_tables.GT.fmt_url`) or
  [`fmt_email()`](`great_tables.GT.fmt_email`)
- `anyfontsize` (optional), so that a `table_font_size=` set with `tab_options()` is used at
  exactly that size rather than the nearest available one

For example, `\usepackage{booktabs}` and `\usepackage{longtable}`. Some currency symbols
(e.g., `"₹"` for `"INR"`) need XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX rather than pdfLaTeX (see
[`fmt_currency()`](`great_tables.GT.fmt_currency`)).

## Limitations {.doc-limitations}

The `as_latex()` method is still experimental and has some limitations. The following
functionality that is supported in HTML output tables is not currently supported in LaTeX
output tables:

- footnotes (via the `tab_footnote()` method), which raise an error
- the `fmt_nanoplot()` method, which raises an error
- the [`fmt_image()`](`great_tables.GT.fmt_image`), `fmt_flag()`, and `fmt_icon()` methods,
  which issue a warning and leave the cell values unformatted
- styles, whether set with the `tab_style()` or `data_color()` methods (a warning is issued
  and the table is rendered without them)
- most options in the `tab_options()` method, particularly those that are specific to styling
  text, borders, or adding fill colors to cells (the ones that are used are `table_width=`,
  `table_font_size=`, `stub_indent_length=`, and `row_group_as_column=`), and so also the
  `opt_*()` methods that set them, such as `opt_stylize()`
- interactive tables (via the `opt_interactive()` method), which are rendered as static
  tables

As development continues, we will work to expand the capabilities of the `as_latex()` method to
reduce these limitations and more clearly document what is and is not supported.

## Examples {.doc-examples}

Let's use a subset of the `gtcars` dataset to create a new table.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT, data
from great_tables.data import gtcars
import polars as pl

gtcars_mini = (
    data.pl.gtcars
    .select(["mfr", "model", "msrp"])
    .head(5)
)

gt_tbl = (
    GT(gtcars_mini)
    .tab_header(
        title="Data Listing from the gtcars Dataset",
        subtitle="Only five rows from the dataset are shown here."
    )
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
)

gt_tbl
```

Now we can return the table as string of LaTeX code using the `as_latex()` method.

```{python}
gt_tbl.as_latex()
```

The LaTeX string contains the code just for the table (it's not a complete LaTeX document).
This output can be useful for embedding a GT table in an existing LaTeX document.


## Pipeline

Sometimes, you might want to programmatically manipulate the table while still benefiting from the chained API that **Great Tables** offers. `pipe()` is designed to tackle this issue.



pipe(self: GT, func: Callable[Concatenate[GT, P], GT], *args: P.args, **kwargs: P.kwargs) -> GT

Provide a structured way to chain a function for a GT object.

::: {.doc-text}

This function accepts a function that receives a GT object along with optional positional and
keyword arguments, returning a GT object. This allows users to easily integrate a function
into the chained API offered by **Great Tables**.
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[func]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Callable[Concatenate[GT, P], GT]]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A function that receives a GT object along with optional positional and keyword arguments,
    returning a GT object.

<code>[*args]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [P.args]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Optional positional arguments to be passed to the function.

<code>[**kwargs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [P.kwargs]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   Optional keyword arguments to be passed to the function.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [gt]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A GT object.
:::

## Examples: {.doc-examples}

Let's use the `name`, `land_area_km2`, and `density_2021` columns of the `towny` dataset to
create a table. First, we'll demonstrate using two consecutive calls to the `.tab_style()`
method to highlight the maximum value of the `land_area_km2` column with `"lightgray"` and the
maximum value of the `density_2021` column with `"lightblue"`.

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, data, loc, style


towny_mini = data.pl.towny.head(10)

(
    GT(
        towny_mini[["name", "land_area_km2", "density_2021"]],
        rowname_col="name",
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="lightgray"),
        locations=loc.body(
            columns="land_area_km2",
            rows=pl.col("land_area_km2").eq(pl.col("land_area_km2").max()),
        ),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="lightblue"),
        locations=loc.body(
            columns="density_2021",
            rows=pl.col("density_2021").eq(pl.col("density_2021").max()),
        ),
    )
)
```

Next, we'll demonstrate how to achieve the same result using the `.pipe()` method to
programmatically style each column.

```{python}
columns = ["land_area_km2", "density_2021"]
colors = ["lightgray", "lightblue"]


def tbl_style(gtbl: GT, columns: list[str], colors: list[str]) -> GT:
    for column, color in zip(columns, colors):
        gtbl = gtbl.tab_style(
            style=style.fill(color=color),
            locations=loc.body(columns=column, rows=pl.col(column).eq(pl.col(column).max())),
        )
    return gtbl


(
    GT(
        towny_mini[["name", "land_area_km2", "density_2021"]],
        rowname_col="name",
    ).pipe(tbl_style, columns, colors)
)
```


## Value Formatting Functions

If you have single values (or lists of them) in need of formatting, we have a set of `val_fmt_*()` functions that have been adapted from the corresponding `fmt_*()` methods.



fmt_number(x: X, decimals: int = 2, n_sigfig: int | None = None, drop_trailing_zeros: bool = False, drop_trailing_dec_mark: bool = True, use_seps: bool = True, accounting: bool = False, scale_by: float = 1, compact: bool = False, pattern: str = '{x}', sep_mark: str = ',', dec_mark: str = '.', force_sign: bool = False, min_sep_threshold: int = 1, locale: str | None = None, system: NumberSystem = 'intl') -> list[str]

Format numeric values.

::: {.doc-text}

With numeric values in a list, we can perform number-based formatting so that the values are
rendered with some level of precision. The following major options are available:

- decimals: choice of the number of decimal places, option to drop trailing zeros, and a choice
of the decimal symbol
- digit grouping separators: options to enable/disable digit separators and provide a choice of
separator symbol
- scaling: we can choose to scale targeted values by a multiplier value
- large-number suffixing: larger figures (thousands, millions, etc.) can be autoscaled and
decorated with the appropriate suffixes
- pattern: option to use a text pattern for decoration of the formatted values
- locale-based formatting: providing a locale ID will result in number formatting specific to
the chosen locale
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[x]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [X]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A list of values to be formatted.

<code>[decimals]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The `decimals` values corresponds to the exact number of decimal places to use. A value such
    as `2.34` can, for example, be formatted with `0` decimal places and it would result in
    `"2"`. With `4` decimal places, the formatted value becomes `"2.3400"`. The trailing zeros
    can be removed with `drop_trailing_zeros=True`. If you always need `decimals = 0`, the
    [`val_fmt_integer()`](`great_tables._formats_vals.val_fmt_integer`) function should be
    considered.

<code>[n_sigfig]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A option to format numbers to *n* significant figures. By default, this is `None` and thus
    number values will be formatted according to the number of decimal places set via
    `decimals`. If opting to format according to the rules of significant figures, `n_sigfig`
    must be a number greater than or equal to `1`. Any values passed to the `decimals` and
    `drop_trailing_zeros` arguments will be ignored.

<code>[drop_trailing_zeros]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A boolean value that allows for removal of trailing zeros (those redundant zeros after the
    decimal mark).

<code>[drop_trailing_dec_mark]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A boolean value that determines whether decimal marks should always appear even if there are
    no decimal digits to display after formatting (e.g., `23` becomes `23.` if `False`). By
    default trailing decimal marks are not shown.

<code>[use_seps]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The `use_seps` option allows for the use of digit group separators. The type of digit group
    separator is set by `sep_mark` and overridden if a locale ID is provided to `locale`. This
    setting is `True` by default.

<code>[accounting]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   An option to use accounting style for values. Normally, negative values will be shown with a
    minus sign but using accounting style will instead put any negative values in parentheses.

<code>[scale_by]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   All numeric values will be multiplied by the `scale_by` value before undergoing formatting.
    Since the `default` value is `1`, no values will be changed unless a different multiplier
    value is supplied.

<code>[compact]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A boolean value that allows for compact formatting of numeric values. Values will be scaled
    and decorated with the appropriate suffixes (e.g., `1230` becomes `1.23K`, and `1230000`
    becomes `1.23M`). The `compact` option is `False` by default. With `system="ind"`, values
    are expressed in lakhs and crores instead (e.g., `1234567` becomes `12.35 Lac`).

<code>[pattern]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;{x}&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A formatting pattern that allows for decoration of the formatted value. The formatted value
    is represented by the `{x}` (which can be used multiple times, if needed) and all other
    characters will be interpreted as string literals.

<code>[sep_mark]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;,&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The string to use as a separator between groups of digits. For example, using `sep_mark=","`
    with a value of `1000` would result in a formatted value of `"1,000"`. This argument is
    ignored if a `locale` is supplied (i.e., is not `None`).

<code>[dec_mark]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;.&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The string to be used as the decimal mark. For example, using `dec_mark=","` with the value
    `0.152` would result in a formatted value of `"0,152"`). This argument is ignored if a
    `locale` is supplied (i.e., is not `None`).

<code>[force_sign]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Should the positive sign be shown for positive values (effectively showing a sign for all
    values except zero)? If so, use `True` for this option. The default is `False`, where only
    negative numbers will display a minus sign.

<code>[min_sep_threshold]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The minimum number of digits in the integer part of a number for digit grouping
    separators to be used. The default of `1` uses separators from 4-digit numbers onward
    (e.g., `1,000`), `2` starts at 5-digit numbers (`10,000`), and `3` starts at 6-digit
    numbers (`100,000`). When a `locale=` value is provided, the locale's own minimum grouping
    digits value is used instead (it's `2` for locales like `"es"` and `"pl"`).

<code>[locale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   An optional locale identifier that can be used for formatting values according the locale's
    rules. Examples include `"en"` for English (United States) and `"fr"` for French (France).

<code>[system]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NumberSystem]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;intl&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The numbering system to use for digit grouping. The international numbering system
    (`"intl"`, the default) always separates groups of three digits (e.g., `"1,234,567"`). The
    Indian numbering system (`"ind"`) separates the last three digits and then groups of two,
    which correspond to thousands, lakhs, crores, and higher quantities (e.g., `"12,34,567"`).
    The separator itself is still set by `sep_mark=` (or the locale) and can be turned off with
    `use_seps=False`.
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [list[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A list of formatted values is returned.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```{python}
from great_tables import vals

vals.fmt_number([0.325, 777000], decimals=2)
```

fmt_integer(x: X, use_seps: bool = True, accounting: bool = False, scale_by: float = 1, compact: bool = False, pattern: str = '{x}', sep_mark: str = ',', force_sign: bool = False, min_sep_threshold: int = 1, locale: str | None = None, system: NumberSystem = 'intl') -> list[str]

Format values as integers.

::: {.doc-text}

With numeric values in a list, we can perform number-based formatting so that the input values

<code>[min_sep_threshold]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

## Examples {.doc-examples}

```{python}
from great_tables import vals

vals.fmt_integer([100000.1, 2000000000.2], use_seps=False)
```

fmt_scientific(x: X, decimals: int = 2, n_sigfig: int | None = None, drop_trailing_zeros: bool = False, drop_trailing_dec_mark: bool = True, scale_by: float = 1, exp_style: str = 'x10n', pattern: str = '{x}', sep_mark: str = ',', dec_mark: str = '.', force_sign_m: bool = False, force_sign_n: bool = False, locale: str | None = None) -> list[str]

Format values to scientific notation.

::: {.doc-text}

With numeric values in a list, we can perform formatting so that the input values are rendered
in scientific notation, where extremely large or very small numbers can be expressed in a more
practical fashion. Here, numbers are written in the form of a mantissa (`m`) and an exponent
(`n`) with the construction *m* x 10^*n* or *m*E*n*. The mantissa component is a number between
`1` and `10`. For instance, `2.5 x 10^9` can be used to represent the value 2,500,000,000 in
scientific notation. In a similar way, 0.00000012 can be expressed as `1.2 x 10^-7`. Due to its
ability to describe numbers more succinctly and its ease of calculation, scientific notation is
widely employed in scientific and technical domains.

We have fine control over the formatting task, with the following options:

- decimals: choice of the number of decimal places, option to drop trailing zeros, and a choice
of the decimal symbol
- scaling: we can choose to scale targeted values by a multiplier value
- pattern: option to use a text pattern for decoration of the formatted values
- locale-based formatting: providing a locale ID will result in formatting specific to the
chosen locale
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[x]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [X]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A list of values to be formatted.

<code>[decimals]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The `decimals` values corresponds to the exact number of decimal places to use. A value such
    as `2.34` can, for example, be formatted with `0` decimal places and it would result in
    `"2"`. With `4` decimal places, the formatted value becomes `"2.3400"`. The trailing zeros
    can be removed with `drop_trailing_zeros=True`.

<code>[n_sigfig]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A option to format numbers to *n* significant figures. By default, this is `None` and thus
    number values will be formatted according to the number of decimal places set via
    `decimals`. If opting to format according to the rules of significant figures, `n_sigfig`
    must be a number greater than or equal to `1`. Any values passed to the `decimals` and
    `drop_trailing_zeros` arguments will be ignored.

<code>[drop_trailing_zeros]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A boolean value that allows for removal of trailing zeros (those redundant zeros after the
    decimal mark).

<code>[drop_trailing_dec_mark]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A boolean value that determines whether decimal marks should always appear even if there are
    no decimal digits to display after formatting (e.g., `23` becomes `23.` if `False`). By
    default trailing decimal marks are not shown.

<code>[scale_by]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   All numeric values will be multiplied by the `scale_by` value before undergoing formatting.
    Since the `default` value is `1`, no values will be changed unless a different multiplier
    value is supplied.

<code>[exp_style]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;x10n&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Style of formatting to use for the scientific notation formatting. By default this is
    `"x10n"` but other options include using a single letter (e.g., `"e"`, `"E"`, etc.), a
    letter followed by a `"1"` to signal a minimum digit width of one, or `"low-ten"` for using
    a stylized `"10"` marker.

<code>[pattern]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;{x}&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   A formatting pattern that allows for decoration of the formatted value. The formatted value
    is represented by the `{x}` (which can be used multiple times, if needed) and all other
    characters will be interpreted as string literals.

<code>[sep_mark]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;,&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The string to use as a separator between groups of digits. For example, using `sep_mark=","`
    with a value of `1000` would result in a formatted value of `"1,000"`. This argument is
    ignored if a `locale` is supplied (i.e., is not `None`).

<code>[dec_mark]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[&quot;.&quot;]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   The string to be used as the decimal mark. For example, using `dec_mark=","` with the value
    `0.152` would result in a formatted value of `"0,152"`). This argument is ignored if a
    `locale` is supplied (i.e., is not `None`).

<code>[force_sign_m]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Should the plus sign be shown for positive values of the mantissa (first component)? This
    would effectively show a sign for all values except zero on the first numeric component of
    the notation. If so, use `True` (the default for this is `False`), where only negative
    numbers will display a sign.

<code>[force_sign_n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   Should the plus sign be shown for positive values of the exponent (second component)? This
    would effectively show a sign for all values except zero on the second numeric component of
    the notation. If so, use `True` (the default for this is `False`), where only negative
    numbers will display a sign.

<code>[locale]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>

:   An optional locale identifier that can be used for formatting values according the locale's
    rules. Examples include `"en"` for English (United States) and `"fr"` for French (France).
:::

## Returns {.doc-returns}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code> [list[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A list of formatted values is returned.
:::

## Examples {.doc-examples}

from great_tables import vals

vals.fmt_scientific([123456, 0.425639], decimals=2)

fmt_engineering(x: X, decimals: int = 2, n_sigfig: int | None = None, drop_trailing_zeros: bool = False, drop_trailing_dec_mark: bool = True, scale_by: float = 1, exp_style: str = 'x10n', pattern: str = '{x}', dec_mark: str = '.', force_sign_m: bool = False, force_sign_n: bool = False, locale: str | None = None) -> list[str]

Format values to engineering notation.

::: {.doc-text}

With numeric values in a list, we can perform formatting so that the input values are rendered
in engineering notation, where numbers are written in the form of a mantissa (`m`) and an
exponent (`n`). When combined the construction is either of the form *m* x 10^*n* or *m*E*n*.
The mantissa is a number between `1` and `1000` and the exponent is a multiple of `3`. For
example, the number `0.0000345` can be written in engineering notation as `34.50 x 10^-6`. This
notation helps to simplify calculations and make it easier to compare numbers that are on very
different scales.

Engineering notation is particularly useful as it aligns with SI prefixes (e.g., *milli-*,
*micro-*, *kilo-*, *mega-*). For instance, numbers in engineering notation with exponent `-3`
correspond to milli-units, while those with exponent `6` correspond to mega-units.

We have fine control over the formatting task, with the following options:

- decimals: choice of the number of decimal places, option to drop trailing zeros, and a choice
of the decimal symbol
- scaling: we can choose to scale targeted values by a multiplier value
- pattern: option to use a text pattern for decoration of the formatted values
- locale-based formatting: providing a locale ID will result in formatting specific to the
chosen locale
:::

fmt_number_si(x: X, unit: str | None = None, decimals: int = 2, n_sigfig: int | None = None, drop_trailing_zeros: bool = False, drop_trailing_dec_mark: bool = True, scale_by: float = 1, prefix_mode: str = 'engineering', pattern: str = '{x}', sep_mark: str = ',', dec_mark: str = '.', force_sign: bool = False, incl_space: bool = True, locale: str | None = None) -> list[str]

Format values with SI (metric) prefixes.

::: {.doc-text}

Format numeric values with SI (International System of Units) prefixes, automatically selecting
the appropriate prefix to keep the mantissa in a readable range. SI prefixes range from quetta
(Q, 10^30) to quecto (q, 10^-30) and are commonly used in scientific and engineering contexts
to represent very large or very small quantities with units (e.g., `"5.2 kW"`, `"3.8 ng"`,
`"1.2 GHz"`, etc.).
:::

## Parameters {.doc-parameters}

::: {.doc-definition-items}
<code>[x]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [X]{.doc-parameter-annotation}</code>

:   A character string specifying the unit to append after the SI prefix (e.g., `"g"` for
    grams, `"W"` for watts, `"Hz"` for hertz, `"m"` for meters). If `None`, only the prefix
    will be shown.

<code>[decimals]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default}</code>
