each style also stripes the body rows (turn this off with `add_row_striping=False`).

## `opt_*()` Convenience Methods

This section shows the different `opt_*()` methods available. They serve as convenience methods for
common `~~GT.tab_options()` tasks.

### Align the Table Header

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_align_table_header(align="left")
```

The title and subtitle are now left-aligned rather than centered, which works well for tables
embedded in text-heavy documents.

### Make Text ALL CAPS

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_all_caps()
```

Column labels, row labels in the stub, and row group labels are rendered in uppercase (and in a
smaller, bolder font), giving the table a more formal, structured appearance.

### Reduce or Expand Padding

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_vertical_padding(scale=0.3)
```

Reducing vertical padding creates a more compact table that fits more data into less vertical space.

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_horizontal_padding(scale=3)
```

Increasing horizontal padding adds breathing room between columns, which improves readability when
columns contain long values.

### Set a Table Outline

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_table_outline()
```

The outline's `style=`, `width=`, and `color=` can all be changed from their defaults (a solid,
`3px`, light gray line).

### Stripe the Rows

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_row_striping()
```

Alternating row backgrounds help the eye follow a row across a wide table.

### Set the Table Font

```{python}
gt_ex.opt_table_font(stack="humanist")
```

The `font=` argument takes one or more font names (or a Google Font via `google_font()`), and
`stack=` takes the name of one of fifteen themed font stacks, like `"humanist"` or
`"monospace-code"`, that have been tested to work across a wide range of systems.

The `opt_*()` methods give you quick access to common styling patterns without needing to remember
the specific `~~GT.tab_options()` argument names. For full control, you can always drop down to
`~~GT.tab_options()` directly, but these convenience methods cover the most frequent customization
needs in just a single method call.

For a theme you write yourself, and for tables that follow light and dark pages, see [Themes and Dark Mode](./17-themes-and-dark-mode.qmd).


### Themes and Dark Mode

A table follows the light or dark look of the page it is shown in, with no code from you. When you
want to change more than that, a `Theme` is a reusable set of colors, fonts, and `~~GT.tab_options()`
values that you apply to one table with `~~GT.opt_theme()`. This page covers the automatic light and
dark behavior, how to write a theme, which value wins when several apply, the CSS variables that make
this work in HTML, and how to build a theme from a [brand.yml](https://posit-dev.github.io/brand-yml/)
file.

The examples use a small piece of `exibble`.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT, Theme, data

small = data.pl.exibble.select("num", "char", "currency", "row")

gt_small = GT(small, rowname_col="row").tab_header("A small table")
```

## Automatic Light and Dark

By default a table is in `"auto"` mode. It is light, and it turns dark when the page around it is
dark. It reads that from two places:

* The page's own theme, when the page is one of these hosts: JupyterLab and Notebook 7, VS Code
  notebooks, Quarto, marimo, or a page using Bootstrap 5.3's `data-bs-theme` attribute. When themes
  are nested, the nearest one wins, so a `data-bs-theme="light"` section of a dark page keeps its
  table light.
* The page's color scheme, the CSS `color-scheme` property. A page declares `dark` to be dark, or
  `light dark` to follow the reader's system setting. The pages that Great Tables makes (with
  `~~GT.show()` or `as_raw_html(make_page=True)`) declare `light dark`.

A page that says neither stays light, so a default table is never dark on a light page.

You do not need to do anything for this. The table below is a default table, so it changes with the
page it is shown in.

```{python}
gt_small
```

`~~GT.opt_theme()` takes a `mode=` to pin the table instead:

* `"light"`: always the light colors.
* `"dark"`: always the dark colors.
* `"auto"`: the default.

```{python}
gt_small.opt_theme(mode="dark")
```

```{python}
gt_small.opt_theme(mode="light")
```

Use `mode="dark"` for a table on a page that is always dark but doesn't say so, and `mode="light"`
for a table that should stay light on a dark page.

A table with a background color set through `~~GT.tab_options()` or `~~GT.opt_stylize()` stays light
in `"auto"` mode. Those colors were picked for a light table, and they apply in both modes, so
switching would give pale stripes on a dark table. `mode="dark"` still forces dark. The same goes for
a background option set in a `Theme`, unless the theme's `dark=` gives that option a value of its own:
then the table has a color for each mode, and it follows the page.

## Writing a Theme

A `Theme` holds values for a few tokens, plus any option that `~~GT.tab_options()` accepts. Give only
what you want to change. Everything else keeps its built-in value.

| Argument        | CSS variable               | What it sets                                                                  |
| --------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `background`    | `--gt-color-background`    | The table background. Sections without a color of their own use it.           |
| `foreground`    | `--gt-color-foreground`    | The text color on that background.                                            |
| `border`        | `--gt-color-border`        | The lines and borders that are light gray (`#D3D3D3`) by default.             |
| `border_strong` | `--gt-color-border-strong` | The top and bottom table borders.                                             |
| `stripe`        | `--gt-color-stripe`        | The background of striped rows.                                               |
| `accent`        | `--gt-color-accent`        | For your own CSS. Interactive tables' controls get it as `--gt-i-accent`.     |
| `font`          | `--gt-font-family`         | The font, one name or a list. It goes ahead of the default font stack.        |
| `font_size`     | `--gt-font-size`           | The base font size, as a CSS length or a number of pixels.                    |

Any other argument is the name of a `~~GT.tab_options()` option, checked the same way. An unknown
name raises an error.

A theme that sets `background` but not `foreground` keeps the built-in text colors, and the table
picks the light or the dark one for that background, as it does for
`~~GT.tab_options(table_background_color=...)`.

```{python}
compact = Theme(
    border="#9AA5B1",
    font="Georgia",
    data_row_padding="3px",
    column_labels_font_weight="bold",
)

gt_small.opt_theme(compact)
```

There are no tokens for spacing, since the default padding differs by table part. Set the padding
options (`data_row_padding`, `column_labels_padding`, and so on) in the theme instead.

A table has one theme at a time: a second `~~GT.opt_theme()` call with a theme replaces the first.
`opt_theme(False)` removes the theme, and leaves the mode as it is.

### Colors for dark mode

`dark=` takes a second `Theme` with the values to use in dark mode. It can hold the five color tokens
(`background`, `foreground`, `border`, `border_strong`, `stripe`) and color options that are written
to the table's stylesheet, such as `table_body_hlines_color`. Anything else (a padding or a font, for
example) raises an error, because it cannot vary by mode in CSS. A `dark` theme cannot have its own `dark=`.

```{python}
navy = Theme(
    border="#9AA5B1",
    font="Georgia",
    dark=Theme(background="#101418", border="#2A3038"),
)

gt_small.opt_theme(navy)
```

The built-in dark theme supplies a background, text, border, strong border, and stripe color. A
theme's light color tokens are not used in dark mode. A theme that sets `background` and has no
`dark=` still goes dark with the built-in dark background, and `mode="light"` keeps it light. Spacing,
fonts, the accent, and any color option the theme sets directly carry over to dark mode unless
`dark=` replaces them. A border or line color that carries over is blended toward the dark text
color, since a color chosen for a light table (black lines, say) would barely show on a dark one. The
same is done for border colors set with `~~GT.tab_options()`. Give the option a value in `dark=` to
choose the dark color yourself.

## What Wins

When several things set the same option, the first of these that exists is used:

1. A value set with `~~GT.tab_options()` or an `opt_*()` method. It applies in both modes (a border
   color is blended in dark mode, as described above).
2. In dark mode, the option in the theme's `dark=`.
3. The option in the theme.
4. In dark mode, for an option fed by a color token: the token in the theme's `dark=`, then the
   built-in dark token.
5. The token in the theme.
6. The built-in value.

Setting an option to its default value with `~~GT.tab_options()` still counts as setting it.

Values from `~~GT.tab_options()` and the `opt_*()` methods are absolute. They are not scaled from the
theme. `~~GT.opt_vertical_padding()`, `~~GT.opt_horizontal_padding()`, and `~~GT.opt_table_font()`
with `add=True` compute from the built-in values, and what they compute then replaces the theme's
value. Below, the theme asks for `3px` of padding, and the `scale=2` in `opt_vertical_padding()`
doubles the built-in `8px`, so the rows get `16px`.

```{python}
gt_small.opt_theme(Theme(data_row_padding="3px")).opt_vertical_padding(scale=2)
```

The order of the calls does not matter. A theme is stored apart from the table's options, so
`~~GT.opt_theme()` before or after `~~GT.tab_options()` gives the same table.

## CSS Variables

In HTML, every option that is written to the table's stylesheet is a CSS variable on that table. The
name is `--gt-` followed by the option name, with underscores turned into hyphens: `data_row_padding`
is `--gt-data-row-padding`, and `table_body_hlines_color` is `--gt-table-body-hlines-color`. The
tokens use the names in the table above. These options are not part of the stylesheet and have no
variable: the footnote marks, order, and spec (`footnotes_marks`, `footnotes_order`,
`footnotes_spec_ref`, `footnotes_spec_ftr`); the source note separator and multiline setting
(`source_notes_sep`, `source_notes_multiline`); the container options (`container_width`,
`container_height`, `container_padding_x`, `container_padding_y`, `container_overflow_x`,
`container_overflow_y`); the Quarto options (`quarto_disable_processing`, `quarto_use_bootstrap`);
the options that say whether a part is included or shown (`table_border_top_include`,
`table_border_bottom_include`, `row_striping_include_stub`, `row_striping_include_table_body`,
`column_labels_hidden`, `row_group_as_column`); `table_id`, `table_caption`, and
`table_additional_css`; and the `ihtml_*` options. `table_font_names` has no variable of its own: it
is written through `--gt-font-family`.

`--gt-color-accent` is not read by any CSS. A static table has no accent, and an interactive table
reads `--gt-i-accent`: a theme's `accent` is written to that variable on the interactive table's
element, and page CSS can set `--gt-i-accent` itself.

A table declares a variable only for a value that was set from Python. Every other value is a
fallback in the CSS, so page CSS can set the variables on a parent of the table, and this works for
anything the Python code left alone. The page below sets a border color and tighter padding on every
table inside `.tight`.

```{=html}
<style>
.tight {
    --gt-color-border: #C0392B;
    --gt-data-row-padding: 2px;
}
</style>
```

::: {.tight}

```{python}
gt_small
```

:::

A value set from Python wins over the page's CSS, because the table declares it on its own element.
In the next table `data_row_padding` is set in Python, so the `2px` from the page CSS is not used,
while the border color from the page still is.

::: {.tight}

```{python}
gt_small.tab_options(data_row_padding="10px")
```

:::

The same holds for a theme: its values count as set from Python. A table cannot be restyled from page
CSS for any value its theme sets.

Text colors are not picked again for a background set in page CSS. Python picks the text color of
each part of the table for the background that part has in Python, so page CSS that sets a background
should set the text color with it. `--gt-color-foreground` is the text color, in both modes, of every
part whose background was not set from Python. The page below makes every table inside `.ink` dark.

```{=html}
<style>
.ink {
    --gt-color-background: #101418;
    --gt-color-foreground: #E6E6E6;
}
</style>
```

::: {.ink}

```{python}
gt_small
```

:::

There is no text color variable for a single part of the table. A part whose background is set only
in page CSS (with `--gt-heading-background-color`, say) keeps the text color picked for the table's
background, so set that background from Python, with `~~GT.tab_options()`, to have its text color
picked for it.

Custom properties are inherited. A table placed inside another table (for example, one pasted into a
cell as raw HTML) reads the variables that Python set on the outer table. The row details of
interactive tables are the exception: the outer table's variables are reset around them. That reset
also blocks page CSS, so a variable that the outer table sets does not reach a table in its row
details from the page either.

## brand.yml

If your organization describes its colors and fonts in a brand.yml file, `Theme.from_brand()` turns
it into a `Theme`. This needs the [brand_yml](https://pypi.org/project/brand-yml/) package, which is
installed with `pip install great_tables[brand]`. Without it, `Theme.from_brand()` raises an
`ImportError` that names the extra.

Take this `_brand.yml`.

```yaml
color:
  palette:
    navy: "#001F3F"
  background: "#FDF6E3"
  foreground: "#073642"
  primary: navy
typography:
  fonts:
    - family: Inter
      source: system
  base:
    family: Inter
    size: 14px
```

Pass its path to `Theme.from_brand()` and apply the result like any other theme.

```python
from great_tables import GT, Theme, data

theme = Theme.from_brand("_brand.yml")

GT(data.pl.exibble).opt_theme(theme)
```

These fields are used:

| brand.yml field          | `Theme` argument |
| ------------------------ | ---------------- |
| `color.background`       | `background`     |
| `color.foreground`       | `foreground`     |
| `color.primary`          | `accent`         |
| `typography.base.family` | `font`           |
| `typography.base.size`   | `font_size`      |

A color that names an entry of `color.palette` becomes that entry's color. A field the file does not
have is left out of the theme. The `border`, `border_strong`, and `stripe` tokens are not taken from
the brand, so they keep their built-in values. Font files and Google Font imports are not loaded; only
the family name is used.

A brand.yml file has one set of colors. For dark mode, pass a second file with `dark=`. Only its
`background` and `foreground` are used, as the colors of the theme's `dark=`.

```python
theme = Theme.from_brand("_brand.yml", dark="_brand-dark.yml")
```

Each argument can also be a `brand_yml.Brand` object. With no argument, `Theme.from_brand()` leaves
the search for a file to `brand_yml`. In `brand_yml` 0.2.0 that needs the `BRAND_YML_PATH`
environment variable to be set, so pass a path when you can.

## Limits

* **Colors you set on cells are not themed.** Literal colors from `~~GT.tab_style()`,
  `~~GT.data_color()`, and `~~GT.opt_stylize()` are written as you gave them, in both modes. A few
  cases are adjusted so the text stays readable:
    * A cell with a fill and no text color gets a text color chosen for contrast with the fill. In
      light mode this changes cells whose fill is dark or mid-tone (red, blue, or green, for example),
      not only dark fills. A text color you write with `style.css()` still wins.
    * A text color on a cell with no fill is blended toward the section's text color in dark mode, and
      is left as written in light mode.
    * A cell with both a fill and a text color is left as written, and so is a fill from
      `~~GT.data_color()` with its defaults.
    * A fill that is translucent or a keyword (`transparent`, `inherit`, and so on) is left alone.
    * `~~GT.data_color(autocolor_text=False)` fills keep the table's text color in light mode. In
      dark mode they get a text color chosen for contrast with the fill, so that light fills don't
      show the table's light text.
    * Border colors from `style.borders()` are blended toward the section's text color in dark mode,
      as text colors are.
    * Email HTML (`inline_css=True`) keeps the text and border colors you set as written, in both modes.
* **Forced dark can lower contrast.** In `mode="dark"`, text on a mid-tone fill that you set (the
  header of an `~~GT.opt_stylize()` table, for example) uses the dark theme's text color. It can have
  lower contrast than in light mode.
* **Content in a cell keeps its own colors.** Plots from extension packages, raw HTML or SVG, and
  images inside a cell are not adapted to dark mode.
* **`as_raw_html()` needs CSS custom properties.** Its output only renders as intended where the
  renderer supports them. `as_raw_html(inline_css=True)` writes literal styles instead, for one mode.
* **Some output has one mode.** Email HTML (`inline_css=True`), images, LaTeX, Word, and Typst output
  cannot follow a preference. In email HTML, `"auto"` gives the light table and `"dark"` the dark
  one. Output made through gridwell (`as_gridwell()`, and `gtsave()` to formats such as SVG or Word)
  and LaTeX ignores the mode and is light, even with `mode="dark"`; the theme values those outputs
  can express, such as border colors, still apply.
* **Quarto renders use literal styles unless the format is HTML.** HTML shown in a Quarto render is
  written the same way as email HTML when the format is not HTML, and for any format when Quarto
  does not report it (older Quarto versions).
* **Iframes and shadow roots do not see the host's theme.** A table in a shadow root follows the
  color scheme it inherits from the page, and a table in an iframe follows the color scheme of the
  iframe's own page (light, if that page does not declare one).
* **Other dark pages get a light table.** Colab and Databricks give no theme signal. Sites built with
  Sphinx or MkDocs may have a dark theme of their own, but the table follows it only if the theme
  sets `color-scheme`. Add `color-scheme: dark` to the page's dark CSS, or use `mode="dark"` if the
  page is always dark.
* **Older browsers show the light table.** Switching needs CSS `light-dark()` (in browsers since
  2024); in a browser without it, an `"auto"` table is always light.


### Nanoplots

:::{.callout-warning}
`~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()` is still experimental.
:::

Nanoplots are tiny plots you can use in your table. They are simple by design, mainly because there
isn't a lot of space to work with. With that simplicity, however, you do get a set of very succinct
data visualizations that adapt nicely to the amount of data you feed into them. The main features of
nanoplots include the following:

- interactivity: you can hover over data and other elements to show values
- choice of line, bar, and box plot charting
- you can annotate plots with a reference line and/or area
- plenty of easy-to-use options for composing your plots

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" arms="up up" cells="12|18|9|24/30|22|35|28/5|14|11|20" cell-trick="nanoplot" intro='[["say", "Tiny plots, right in the cells!"], ["mood", "grin"], ["wait", 400], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

Nanoplots shine when you want to show trends or distributions alongside other tabular data, so the
reader can correlate a visual pattern with the row's other values at a glance. They are not a
replacement for full-sized charts but should instead be used when the visual is supplementary
context rather than the primary message. If a chart needs its own axis labels, legend, or detailed
annotations, it belongs in a standalone figure. But when a compact sparkline or bar sequence adds
meaning to a row without pulling the reader out of the table, a nanoplot is the right tool.

## A Simple Line-Based Nanoplot

Let's make some simple plots with a Polars DataFrame. Here we are using lists to define data values
for each cell in the `numbers` column. The `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()` method understands that these are
input values for a line plot (the default type of nanoplot).

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT

random_numbers_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "example": ["Row " + str(x) for x in range(1, 5)],
        "numbers": [
            "20 23 6 7 37 23 21 4 7 16",
            "2.3 6.8 9.2 2.42 3.5 12.1 5.3 3.6 7.2 3.74",
            "-12 -5 6 3.7 0 8 -7.4",
            "2 0 15 7 8 10 1 24 17 13 6",
        ],
    }
)

GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers")
```

This looks a lot like the familiar sparklines you might see in tables where space for plots is
limited. The input values, strings of space-separated values, can be considered here as *y* values
and they are evenly spaced along the imaginary *x* axis.

Hovering over (or touching) the values is something of a treat! You might notice that:

- data values are automatically formatted for you in a compact fashion
- the plot elements also display pertinent values

This sort of interactivity is baked into the rendered SVG graphics that `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()`
generates from your data and selection of options.

Polars lets us express 'lists-of-values-per-cell' in different ways and **Great Tables** is pretty
good at understanding different column *dtypes*. So, you can alternatively create the same table as
above with the following code.

```python
random_numbers_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "example": ["Row " + str(x) for x in range(1, 5)],
        "numbers": [
            { "val": [20, 23, 6, 7, 37, 23, 21, 4, 7, 16] },
            { "val": [2.3, 6.8, 9.2, 2.42, 3.5, 12.1, 5.3, 3.6, 7.2, 3.74] },
            { "val": [-12, -5, 6, 3.7, 0, 8, -7.4] },
            { "val": [2, 0, 15, 7, 8, 10, 1, 24, 17, 13, 6] },
        ],
    }
)

GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers")
```

Both forms of the `numbers` column in the two DataFrames look the same to `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()`. The
key for the list of values (here, `"val"`) can be anything as long as it's repeated down the column.
So the choice is yours on how you want to prepare those column values.

## The Reference Line and the Reference Area

You can insert two additional things which may be useful: a reference line and a reference area. You
can define them either through literal values or via keywords (these are: `"mean"`, `"median"`,
`"min"`, `"max"`, `"q1"`, `"q3"`, `"first"`, or `"last"`). Here's a reference line that corresponds
to the mean data value of each nanoplot:

```{python}
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", reference_line="mean")
```

This example uses a reference area that bounds the minimum value to the median value:

```{python}
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", reference_area=["min", "median"])
```

As an added touch, you don't need to worry about the order of the keywords provided to
`reference_area=` (which could be potentially problematic if providing a literal value and a
keyword).

## Using `autoscale=` to Have a Common *y*-Axis Scale Across Plots

There are lots of options. Like, if you want to ensure that the scale is shared across all of the
nanoplots (so you can better get a sense of overall magnitude), you can set `autoscale=` to `True`:

```{python}
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", autoscale=True)
```

If you hover along or touch the left side of any of the plots above, you'll see that each *y* scale
runs from `-12.0` to `37.0`. Using `autoscale=True` is very useful if you want to compare the
magnitudes of values across rows in addition to their trends. It won't, however, make much sense if
the overall magnitudes of values vary wildly across rows (e.g., comparing changing currency values
or stock prices over time).

Keep in mind the tradeoff: `autoscale=True` sacrifices within-row detail for cross-row
comparability. If some rows have values in the thousands and others in single digits, autoscaling
may compress the smaller series into a nearly flat line, hiding their internal variation. In those
cases, independent scales (the default) are a better choice because they let each row's nanoplot use
its full vertical range to show that row's own pattern.

## Using the `nanoplot_options()`{.qd-no-link} Helper Function

There are many options for customization. You can radically change the look of a collection of
nanoplots with the `nanoplot_options()` helper function. With that function, you invoke it in the
`options=` argument of `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()`. You can modify the sizes and colors of different
elements, decide which elements are even present, and much more! Here's an example where a
line-based nanoplot retains all of its elements, but the overall appearance is greatly altered.

```{python}
from great_tables import nanoplot_options

(
    GT(random_numbers_df)
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="numbers",
        options=nanoplot_options(
            data_point_radius=8,
            data_point_stroke_color="black",
            data_point_stroke_width=2,
            data_point_fill_color="white",
            data_line_type="straight",
            data_line_stroke_color="brown",
            data_line_stroke_width=2,
            data_area_fill_color="orange",
            vertical_guide_stroke_color="green",
        ),
    )
)
```

As can be seen, you have a lot of fine-grained control over the look of a nanoplot.

## Making Nanoplots with Bars Using `plot_type="bar"`

We don't just support line plots in `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()`, we also have the option to show bar
plots. The only thing you need to change is the value of the `plot_type=` argument to `"bar"`.

Choosing between line and bar nanoplots depends on what you want to emphasize. Line plots highlight
trends and continuity over time or a sequence. And they make it easy to see whether values are
rising, falling, or oscillating. Bar plots, on the other hand, emphasize individual values and make
it straightforward to compare magnitudes across positions. Bar plots also handle negative values
more naturally, with bars projecting downward from a zero line, giving the reader an immediate sense
of sign and scale.

```{python}
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", plot_type="bar")
```

An important difference between line plots and bar plots is that the bars project from a zero line.
Notice that some negative values in the bar-based nanoplot appear red and radiate downward from the
gray zero line.

Using `plot_type="bar"` still allows us to supply a reference line and a reference area with
`reference_line=` and `reference_area=`. The `autoscale=` option works here as well. We also have a
set of options just for bar plots available inside `nanoplot_options()`. Here's an example where we
use all of the aforementioned customization possibilities:

```{python}
(
    GT(random_numbers_df)
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="numbers",
        plot_type="bar",
        autoscale=True,
        reference_line="min",
        reference_area=[0, "max"],
        options=nanoplot_options(
            data_bar_stroke_color="gray",
            data_bar_stroke_width=2,
            data_bar_fill_color="orange",
            data_bar_negative_stroke_color="blue",
            data_bar_negative_stroke_width=1,
            data_bar_negative_fill_color="lightblue",
            reference_line_color="pink",
            reference_area_fill_color="bisque",
            vertical_guide_stroke_color="blue",
        ),
    )
)
```

The customized bars use orange fills, gray strokes, and a pink reference line. Negative values are
styled separately with blue strokes and light blue fills, making it easy to distinguish positive and
negative trends at a glance.

## Horizontal Bar and Line Plots

Single-value bar plots, running in the horizontal direction, can be made by simply invoking
`~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()` on a column of numeric values. These plots are meant for comparison across
rows so the method automatically scales the horizontal bars to facilitate this type of display.
Here's a simple example that uses `plot_type="bar"` on the `numbers` column that contains a single
numeric value in every cell.

```{python}
single_vals_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "example": ["Row " + str(x) for x in range(1, 5)],
        "numbers": [2.75, 0, -3.2, 8]
    }
)

GT(single_vals_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", plot_type="bar")
```

This, interestingly enough, works with the `"line"` type of nanoplot. The result is akin to a
lollipop plot:

```{python}
GT(single_vals_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers")
```

You get to customize the line and the data point marker with the latter display of single values,
and that's a plus. Nonetheless, it is more common to see horizontal bar plots in tables and the
extra customization of negative values makes that form of presentation more advantageous.

## Box Plots Using `plot_type="boxplot"`

When the distribution of values matters more than their order, a box plot is the better choice.
With `plot_type="boxplot"`, each row's values become a horizontal box running from the first to the
third quartile, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend to the most extreme values that are
within 1.5 times the box's width, and any values further out are outliers. Rows with fewer than 20
values also show every value as a faint point. Hovering over (or touching) a box shows the five
statistics.

```{python}
GT(random_numbers_df).fmt_nanoplot(columns="numbers", plot_type="boxplot")
```

Unlike the other nanoplots, box plots always share a scale across rows, so the boxes can be
compared directly. The scale is horizontal, so a reference line or area is drawn vertically. Here's
an example with the `pizzaplace` dataset, where the times of a year's worth of pizza orders are
grouped by weekday. The order times are seconds after midnight, so we provide a formatter to
`nanoplot_options()` that shows them as clock times. A reference area marks the lunch hours.

```{python}
from great_tables import data


def clock(seconds):
    seconds = round(seconds)
    return f"{seconds // 3600:02}:{seconds % 3600 // 60:02}"


order_times = (
    data.pl.pizzaplace
    .with_columns(
        day=pl.col("date").str.to_date().dt.strftime("%A"),
        day_num=pl.col("date").str.to_date().dt.weekday(),
        seconds=pl.col("time").str.to_time().cast(pl.Int64) // 1_000_000_000,
    )
    .group_by("day", "day_num")
    .agg(pizzas=pl.len(), seconds=pl.col("seconds"))
    .sort("day_num")
    .drop("day_num")
)

(
    GT(order_times, rowname_col="day")
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="seconds",
        plot_type="boxplot",
        reference_area=[12 * 3600, 14 * 3600],
        options=nanoplot_options(y_val_fmt_fn=clock),
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns="pizzas")
    .cols_label(pizzas="Pizzas", seconds="Time of order")
)
```

The box plots show that weekend orders come in later in the day than weekday orders. In
`nanoplot_options()`, the box and whiskers take their color and width from
`data_bar_stroke_color=` and `data_bar_stroke_width=`, the box's thickness grows with
`data_point_radius=`, and `show_data_points=False` hides the points.

## Line Plots with Paired *x* and *y* Values

Aside from a single stream of *y* values, we can plot pairs of *x* and *y* values. This works only
for the `"line"` type of plot. We can set up a column of Polars `struct` values in a DataFrame to
have this input data prepared for `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()`. Notice that the dictionary values in the
enclosed list must have the `"x"` and `"y"` keys. Further to this, the list lengths for each of
`"x"` and `"y"` must match (i.e., to make valid pairs of *x* and *y*).

```{python}
weather_2 = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "station": ["Station " + str(x) for x in range(1, 4)],
        "temperatures": [
            {
                "x": [6.1, 8.0, 10.1, 10.5, 11.2, 12.4, 13.1, 15.3],
                "y": [24.2, 28.2, 30.2, 30.5, 30.5, 33.1, 33.5, 32.7],
            },
            {
                "x": [7.1, 8.2, 10.3, 10.75, 11.25, 12.5, 13.5, 14.2],
                "y": [18.2, 18.1, 20.3, 20.5, 21.4, 21.9, 23.1, 23.3],
            },
            {
                "x": [6.3, 7.1, 10.3, 11.0, 12.07, 13.1, 15.12, 16.42],
                "y": [15.2, 17.77, 21.42, 21.63, 25.23, 26.84, 27.2, 27.44],
            },
        ]
    }
)

(
    GT(weather_2)
    .fmt_nanoplot(
        columns="temperatures",
        plot_type="line",
        expand_x=[5, 16],
        expand_y=[10, 40],
        options=nanoplot_options(
            show_data_area=False,
            show_data_line=False
        )
    )
)
```

The options for removing the *data area* and the *data line* (through the corresponding `show_*`
arguments of `nanoplot_options()`) make the finalized nanoplots look somewhat like scatter plots.

Nanoplots bring data visualization directly into your table cells, giving readers an immediate
visual sense of trends and distributions without leaving the tabular format. Between line plots, bar
charts, box plots, reference annotations, and extensive customization through `nanoplot_options()`,
you can tailor these compact visualizations to match your data and your presentation style.



## Advanced Topics

### Column Selection

Many **Great Tables** methods accept a `columns=` argument for targeting specific columns. Rather
than limiting you to a simple list of column names, the package supports a flexible selection system
that includes positional indexing, pattern-matching functions, and Polars selectors. This page
demonstrates each of these approaches.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="thinking" arms="up rest" cells="date|temp|time|wind/May 1|18.9|00:20|6.7/May 1|17.8|00:50|7.2" cell-trick="columns" intro='[["say", "Which columns should I pick?"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

As your table-building code grows, hardcoding column names becomes fragile. If a column is renamed
or added upstream, your table code breaks silently or raises an error. Pattern-based selection
(whether through functions or Polars selectors) makes your code more resilient to upstream changes
and more expressive about intent. Instead of listing every column by name, you can declare
*what kind* of columns you want (e.g., all numeric columns, all columns starting with a prefix), and
the selection adapts automatically as the data evolves.

## Selection Options

The `columns=` argument for methods like `~~GT.tab_spanner()`, `~~GT.cols_move()`, and
`~~GT.tab_style()` allows a range of options for selecting columns.

The simplest approach is just a list of strings with the exact column names. However, we can specify
columns using any of the following:

* a single string column name.
* an integer for the column's position.
* a list of strings or integers.
* a **Polars** selector.
* a function that takes a string and returns `True` or `False`.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT, data

lil_exibble = data.pl.exibble.select("num", "char", "fctr", "date", "time").head(4)
gt_ex = GT(lil_exibble)

gt_ex
```

This five-column table will serve as the basis for demonstrating each selection approach.

## Using Strings and Integers

We can use a list of strings or integers to select columns by name or position, respectively.

```{python}
gt_ex.cols_move_to_start(columns=["date", 1, -1])
```

Note the code above moved the following columns:

* The string `"date"` matched the column of the same name.
* The integer `1` matched the second column (this is similar to list indexing).
* The integer `-1` matched the last column.

Moreover, the order of the list defines the order of selected columns. In this case, `"date"` was
the first entry, so it's the very first column in the new table.

## Using **Polars** Selectors

When using a **Polars** DataFrame, you can select columns using
[**Polars** selectors](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/selectors.html).
The example below uses **Polars** selectors to move all columns that start with `"c"` or `"f"` to
the start of the table.

```{python}
import polars.selectors as cs

gt_ex.cols_move_to_start(columns=cs.starts_with("c") | cs.starts_with("f"))
```

In general, selection should match the behaviors of the **Polars** `DataFrame.select()` method.

```{python}
lil_exibble.select(cs.starts_with("c") | cs.starts_with("f")).columns
```

See the [Selectors page in the Polars docs](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/selectors.html)
for more information on this.

## Using Functions

A function can be used to select columns. It should take a column name as a string and return `True`
or `False`.

```{python}
gt_ex.cols_move_to_start(columns=lambda x: "c" in x)
```

To summarize when to reach for each approach: use a plain list of names when you know exactly which
columns you want and the list is short. Use Polars selectors when you want to match by dtype,
prefix, suffix, or other structural properties of the columns. Use a function when you need custom
logic that doesn't fit neatly into a selector (e.g., matching against an external list or applying a
complex naming convention rule).

These selection methods work consistently across all **Great Tables** methods that accept a
`columns=` argument. Whether you prefer explicit column names, positional indexing, Polars
selectors, or custom functions, you can choose the approach that best fits your workflow and data.


### Row Selection

Just as you can target specific columns, **Great Tables** also provides flexible ways to select
rows. The `rows=` argument appears in formatting methods, location specifiers, and styling calls,
allowing you to apply operations to a precise subset of your data. This page covers each of the
available selection mechanisms.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="wink" arms="open rest" cells="CAN|Canada|38.9M|2023/FRA|France|68.2M|2023/JPN|Japan|125M|2023" cell-trick="rows" intro='[["say", "Any rows you like, I’ll pick them!"], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

Row selection matters because many table operations (formatting, styling, footnotes) need to target
specific rows. Without it, you would need to pre-filter your DataFrame or apply formatting to an
entire column and then somehow undo it for the rows that don't apply. Row selection keeps the logic
in the table layer, close to where it's used, so your data preparation stays clean and your
formatting intent is expressed declaratively alongside the styling calls.

## Selection Options

Location and formatter functions (e.g. `loc.body()` and `~~GT.fmt_number()`) can be applied to
specific rows, using the `rows=` argument.

Rows may be specified using any of the following:

* `None` (the default), to select everything.
* an integer for the row's position.
* a list of integers.
* a **Polars** expression for filtering.
* a function that takes a DataFrame and returns a boolean Series.

The following sections will use a subset of the `exibble` data to demonstrate these options.

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, data, loc, style

lil_exibble = data.pl.exibble.select("num", "char", "currency").head(3)
gt_ex = GT(lil_exibble)
```

## Using Integers

Use a single integer, or a list of integers, to select rows by position.

```{python}
gt_ex.fmt_currency("currency", rows=0, decimals=1)
```

Notice that a dollar sign (`$`) was only added to the first row (index `0` in Python).

Indexing works the same as selecting items from a Python list. This means that negative integers
select relative to the final row.

```{python}
gt_ex.fmt_currency("currency", rows=[0, -1], decimals=1)
```

The first and last rows now show currency formatting, while the middle row remains unchanged.
Negative indices count backward from the end, just as with Python lists.

## Using Polars Expressions

The `rows=` argument accepts Polars expressions, which return a boolean Series indicating which rows
to operate on.

For example, the code below formats the `num` column, but only when `currency` is less than 40.

```{python}
gt_ex.fmt_integer("num", rows=pl.col("currency") < 40)
```

Here's a more realistic example, which highlights the row with the highest value for currency.

```{python}
import polars.selectors as cs

gt_ex.tab_style(
    style.fill("yellow"),
    loc.body(
        columns=cs.all(),
        rows=pl.col("currency") == pl.col("currency").max()
    )
)
```

The row with the maximum currency value is highlighted with a yellow background. Using expressions
for row selection keeps the logic declarative and close to the styling call.

Expression-based row selection is especially powerful for conditional formatting, where the styling
rule depends on the data itself. For example, you can highlight rows where a metric exceeds a
threshold, format only the rows that contain the maximum or minimum value, or apply different styles
based on category membership (all without any imperative filtering logic).

## Using a Function

Since libraries like Pandas don't have lazy expressions, the `rows=` argument also accepts a
function for selecting rows. The function should take a DataFrame and return a boolean Series. A
missing value in that Series leaves its row unselected, as it does with a Polars expression.

Here's the same example as the previous Polars section, but with Pandas data and a lambda for
selecting rows.

```{python}
gt_ex_pd = GT(data.pd.exibble[["num", "char", "currency"]].head(3))

gt_ex_pd.fmt_integer("num", rows=lambda D: D["currency"] < 40)
```

Here's the styling example from the previous Polars section.

```{python}
gt_ex_pd.tab_style(
    style.fill("yellow"),
    loc.body(
        columns=lambda colname: True,
        rows=lambda D: D["currency"] == D["currency"].max()
    )
)
```

Whether you prefer integer indexing for quick positional access, Polars expressions for declarative
filtering, or functions for compatibility with Pandas, the `rows=` argument adapts to your data
workflow. Combined with column selection, these tools give you fine-grained control over exactly
which cells your formatting and styling operations affect.


### Location Selection

The `loc` module is what connects your styling intentions to specific parts of the table. Each
location specifier identifies a region of the table (such as the header, body, stub, or footer) and
many of them also support targeting specific columns or rows within that region. This page provides
a comprehensive overview of all available location specifiers and how to use them effectively.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="thinking" arms="point rest" cells="|temp|hum|wind/GIB|18.9|68%|6.7/MAD|24.1|41%|3.2" cell-trick="locations" intro='[["say", "Which part should we style?"], ["mood", "grin"], ["wait", 400], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

Understanding the `loc` module is valuable because it provides a single, consistent vocabulary for
addressing any part of the table. Rather than learning separate APIs for styling the header vs. the
body vs. the stub, you use the same `loc.*()` specifiers everywhere. This means that once you know
how to style a column label, the pattern for styling a row group label or a source note is
immediately familiar.

## Overview

**Great Tables** uses the `loc` module to specify locations for styling in `~~GT.tab_style()`. Some
location specifiers also allow selecting specific columns and rows of data.

For example, you might style a particular row name, group, column, or spanner label.

The table below shows the different location specifiers, along with the types of column or row
selection they allow.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT

loc_rows = [
    ["header", "loc.header()", "composite"],
    ["", "loc.title()", ""],
    ["", "loc.subtitle()", ""],
    ["stubhead", "loc.stubhead()", ""],
    ["boxhead", "loc.column_header()", "composite"],
    ["", "loc.spanner_labels()", "columns"],
    ["", "loc.column_labels()", "columns"],
    ["row stub", "loc.stub()", "rows"],
    ["", "loc.row_groups()", "rows"],
    ["", "loc.summary_stub()", "groups and rows"],
    ["", "loc.grand_summary_stub()", "rows"],
    ["table body", "loc.body()", "columns, rows, and mask"],
    ["", "loc.summary()", "groups, columns, and rows"],
    ["", "loc.grand_summary()", "columns, rows, and mask"],
    ["footer", "loc.footer()", "composite"],
    ["", "loc.footnotes()", ""],
    ["", "loc.source_notes()", ""],
]

loc_df = pl.DataFrame(loc_rows, schema=["table part", "name", "selection"], orient="row")

GT(loc_df)
```

Note that composite specifiers are ones that target multiple locations. For example, `loc.header()`
specifies both `loc.title()` and `loc.subtitle()`.

## Setting Up the Data

The examples below will use this small dataset to show selecting different locations, as well as
specific rows and columns within a location (where supported).

```{python}
import polars as pl
import polars.selectors as cs

from great_tables import GT, data, loc, style

pl_exibble = data.pl.exibble[[0, 1, 4], ["num", "char", "group"]]

pl_exibble
```

This small three-row, three-column dataset gives us enough structure to demonstrate row and column
targeting without cluttering the output.

## Simple Locations

Simple locations don't take any arguments.

For example, styling the title uses `loc.title()`.

```{python}
(
    GT(pl_exibble)
    .tab_header("A title", "A subtitle")
    .tab_style(
        style.fill("yellow"),
        loc.title(),
    )
)
```

Only the title receives the yellow fill; the subtitle and the rest of the table remain unstyled.
Simple locations are useful when you want precise control over a single element.

## Composite Locations

Composite locations target multiple simple locations.

For example, `loc.header()` includes both `loc.title()` and `loc.subtitle()`.

```{python}
(
    GT(pl_exibble)
    .tab_header("A title", "A subtitle")
    .tab_style(
        style.fill("yellow"),
        loc.header(),
    )
)
```

Both the title and subtitle are filled with yellow because `loc.header()` targets the entire header
region. Composite locations are a convenient shorthand when you want the same style on all
sub-parts.

## Body Columns, Rows, and Mask

Use `columns=` and `rows=` in `loc.body()` to style specific cells in the table body.

```{python}
(
    GT(pl_exibble).tab_style(
        style.fill("yellow"),
        loc.body(
            columns=cs.starts_with("cha"),
            rows=pl.col("char").str.contains("a"),
        ),
    )
)
```

Alternatively, use `mask=` in `loc.body()` to apply conditional styling to rows on a per-column
basis.

```{python}
(
    GT(pl_exibble).tab_style(
        style.fill("yellow"),
        loc.body(mask=cs.string().str.contains("p")),
    )
)
```

This is discussed in detail in [Styling the Table Body](./12-styling-the-table-body.qmd).

## Column Labels

Locations like `loc.spanner_labels()` and `loc.column_labels()` can select specific column and
spanner labels.

You can use name strings, index positions, or Polars selectors.

```{python}
GT(pl_exibble).tab_style(
    style.fill("yellow"),
    loc.column_labels(
        cs.starts_with("cha"),
    ),
)
```

However, note that `loc.spanner_labels()` currently only accepts a list of spanner IDs.

## Row and Group Names

Row and group names in `loc.stub()` and `loc.row_groups()` may be specified three ways:

* by name
* by index
* by Polars expression

```{python}
gt_stub = GT(pl_exibble).tab_stub(
    rowname_col="char",
    groupname_col="group",
)

gt_stub.tab_style(style.fill("yellow"), loc.stub())
```

All row labels in the stub are highlighted in yellow.

```{python}
gt_stub.tab_style(style.fill("yellow"), loc.stub("banana"))
```

Only the `"banana"` row label is styled, demonstrating name-based targeting.

```{python}
gt_stub.tab_style(style.fill("yellow"), loc.stub(["apricot", 2]))
```

You can mix names and integer indices in a list to target multiple specific rows at once.

### Groups by Name and Position

Note that for specifying row groups, the group corresponding to the group name or row number in the
original data is used.

For example, the code below styles the group corresponding to the row at index 1 (i.e., the second
row) in the data.

```{python}
gt_stub.tab_style(
    style.fill("yellow"),
    loc.row_groups(1),
)
```

Since the second row (starting with "banana") is in "grp_a", that is the group that gets styled.

This means you can use a Polars expression to select groups:

```{python}
gt_stub.tab_style(
    style.fill("yellow"),
    loc.row_groups(pl.col("group") == "grp_b"),
)
```

You can also specify group names using a string (or list of strings).

```{python}
gt_stub.tab_style(
    style.fill("yellow"),
    loc.row_groups("grp_b"),
)
```

The `loc` module provides a complete vocabulary for addressing any part of your table. By combining
location specifiers with column selectors, row filters, and Polars expressions, you can apply styles
to exactly the right cells. For more details on styling itself, see
[Styling the Table Body](./12-styling-the-table-body.qmd) and
[Styling the Whole Table](./13-styling-the-whole-table.qmd).


### Exporting and Saving Tables

Once you have built a table, you need to get it into its final destination. That might be a notebook
cell, a standalone HTML file, a LaTeX document, or an image file for inclusion in a report or
presentation. **Great Tables** provides several export methods to cover these use cases, each with
options to control the output format.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" cell-trick="slots" intro='[["arms", "open"], ["write", ["HTML", "PNG", "PDF", "LaTeX", "SVG", "Word", "Excel", "PPT", "RTF", "Typst"], 160], ["mood", "grin"], ["say", "Build once, export many ways!"], ["mood", "happy"], ["arms", "rest"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

The general principle is: build your table once, export it many ways. The same `GT` object can be
displayed interactively, saved as HTML, rendered as LaTeX, or captured as an image. This means you
don't need to maintain separate table-building code for different output formats. Your single chain
of formatting, styling, and structural methods produces the canonical table, and the export step
simply serializes it for the target medium.

## Displaying Tables

In most notebook environments (Jupyter, Quarto, marimo), simply placing a `GT` object as the last
expression in a cell will render the table automatically. However, you can also use the
`~~GT.show()` method for explicit control over where the table is displayed.

```{python}
from great_tables import GT, data

gt_tbl = (
    GT(data.pl.exibble.head(3).select("num", "char", "currency"))
    .tab_header(title="Example Table", subtitle="A small demonstration")
    .fmt_currency(columns="currency")
    .fmt_number(columns="num", decimals=2)
)

gt_tbl.show()
```

The `target=` argument controls the display destination. The available options are:

- `"auto"` (the default): displays inline in a notebook if possible, otherwise opens a browser
window.
- `"notebook"`: forces inline notebook display.
- `"browser"`: opens the table in your default web browser. This is particularly useful when working
in the console or when you want to see the full styled output that some IDEs may suppress.

```python
# Open in a browser window (useful when running from a script or console)
gt_tbl.show(target="browser")
```

## Getting HTML as a String

The `~~GT.as_raw_html()` method returns the table as an HTML string. This is useful for embedding
tables in web applications, email templates, or custom HTML documents. Body cells that have not been
processed by a `fmt_*()` method are automatically HTML-escaped to prevent cross-site scripting (XSS)
when rendering untrusted data. See the [Formatting Values](./08-formatting-values.qmd) page for
details on how to include raw HTML in cells using `html()` and `fmt()`.

```{python}
html_str = gt_tbl.as_raw_html()

# Show the first 200 characters to see the structure
print(html_str[:200])
```

The method accepts several arguments that control the output format.

### Inline CSS for Email

Email clients typically strip `<style>` blocks, so you need inline CSS for the table to render
correctly. Set `inline_css=True` to move all styles into `style` attributes.

```python
email_html = gt_tbl.as_raw_html(inline_css=True)
```

With inline CSS, your table will render correctly in Gmail, Outlook, and other email clients that
strip external stylesheets.

This matters because most email clients aggressively strip `<style>` blocks and external CSS
references for security reasons. Without inline CSS, your carefully styled table will appear as
plain, unstyled HTML in the recipient's inbox. If you are sharing tables via email (whether through
automated reports or one-off sends), `inline_css=True` is almost always what you want.

### Complete HTML Page

If you need a self-contained HTML document (with `<html>`, `<head>`, and `<body>` tags), set
`make_page=True`.

```python
full_page = gt_tbl.as_raw_html(make_page=True)
```

This wraps the table in a complete HTML document that can be opened directly in any browser without
additional scaffolding.

### Writing HTML to a File

The `~~GT.write_raw_html()` method is a convenience wrapper that writes the HTML output directly to
a file (with UTF-8 encoding by default).

```python
gt_tbl.write_raw_html("my_table.html")
```

It takes the same options as `as_raw_html()` (`inline_css=`, `make_page=`, `all_important=`, and
for an interactive table, `runtime=`), so the file can hold an email-ready fragment or a complete
page.

## LaTeX Output

For inclusion in LaTeX documents, the `~~GT.as_latex()` method generates a LaTeX fragment containing
the table.

```{python}
latex_str = gt_tbl.as_latex()
print(latex_str)
```

The output uses a `tabular` environment by default. For tables that span multiple pages, you can
switch to the `longtable` environment.

```python
long_latex = gt_tbl.as_latex(use_longtable=True)
```

The `tbl_pos=` argument controls the float placement when not using `longtable`. Valid options
include `"!t"` (top), `"!b"` (bottom), `"!h"` (here), and `"!H"` (exactly here, requires the
`float` package).

```python
positioned_latex = gt_tbl.as_latex(tbl_pos="!h")
```

:::{.callout-note}
LaTeX output is still experimental. Not all table features (such as certain styling options) are
fully supported in the LaTeX renderer; the *Limitations* section of `~~GT.as_latex()` lists them.
:::

The LaTeX fragment relies on a few LaTeX packages, so load them in your document's preamble:
`booktabs` is always needed, `longtable` is needed with `use_longtable=True`, and `hyperref` is
needed for links from `~~GT.fmt_url()` or `~~GT.fmt_email()`. Adding `anyfontsize` lets a font size
set with `~~GT.tab_options()` be used exactly:

```latex
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{longtable}
\usepackage{hyperref}
\usepackage{anyfontsize}
```

LaTeX output is the bridge between **Great Tables** and the world of academic publishing and
typesetting. If you are writing papers in LaTeX or producing PDF reports via Quarto, this method
lets you bring your Python-built tables into that workflow without manual conversion. You get the
convenience of building tables programmatically in Python with the typographic quality of LaTeX's
table rendering.

## Saving as an Image

The `~~GT.gtsave()` method renders your table as a high-quality image file. It supports PNG, JPEG,
WebP, and PDF formats. Under the hood, it uses the `nokap` package to drive a headless Chrome
browser for pixel-perfect rendering.

```python
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.png")
```

The output format is determined by the file extension (a file name without one is saved as PNG).
The supported formats are:

- `.png` for lossless raster images (great for reports and presentations)
- `.pdf` for vector output (ideal for print and LaTeX inclusion)
- `.jpeg` or `.jpg` for compressed raster images
- `.webp` for efficient web-optimized images

### Controlling Image Quality

The `zoom=` argument controls the resolution of raster outputs. The default value of `2.0` produces
retina-quality images. Increase it for even higher resolution, or decrease it for smaller file
sizes.

```python
# High-resolution image for print
gt_tbl.gtsave("high_res.png", zoom=4.0)

# Standard resolution for web
gt_tbl.gtsave("standard.png", zoom=1.0)
```

A `zoom=4.0` value produces an image with twice the resolution of the default, which is ideal for
print materials where crisp text is essential. The `zoom=` setting doesn't apply to PDF output,
which is already vector-based.

### Padding Around the Table

The `expand=` argument adds padding (in pixels) around the captured table element (the default is
`5`). You can provide a single integer for uniform padding or a tuple of four values for
`(top, right, bottom, left)`.

```python
# Uniform padding
gt_tbl.gtsave("padded.png", expand=20)

# Asymmetric padding
gt_tbl.gtsave("asymmetric.png", expand=(10, 20, 10, 20))
```

Adding padding is especially useful when the saved image will be placed on a colored background or
inside a slide layout where the table edge needs breathing room.

### Viewport Dimensions

The `vwidth=` and `vheight=` arguments set the virtual viewport size. This can affect how responsive
table layouts are rendered (the defaults are `992` and `744` pixels).

```python
gt_tbl.gtsave("wide_viewport.png", vwidth=1200)
```

A wider viewport can prevent the table from wrapping or truncating columns, while a narrower one can
test how the table responds to constrained width.

### Rendering Delay

Some tables with custom fonts or dynamic content may need a short delay after page load before the
screenshot is taken. The `delay=` argument (in seconds, defaulting to `0.2`) controls this wait
time.

```python
gt_tbl.gtsave("with_delay.png", delay=0.5)
```

:::{.callout-note}
For images and PDF, the `gtsave()` method requires the `nokap` package and a Chrome or Chromium
browser to be installed on your system.
:::

## Saving as SVG, Word, Excel, and More

The `~~GT.gtsave()` method also saves a table as SVG, a Word document, an Excel workbook, a
PowerPoint presentation, RTF, or Typst. These files are written by
[gridwell](https://github.com/rich-iannone/gridwell), which draws the same table, with its
formatting and styles, in each format's own terms (as far as each format allows), with no browser
involved. Install it with the `gridwell` extra:

```bash
pip install "great_tables[gridwell]"
```

Then choose the format by the file extension, just as with images:

```python
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.svg")   # SVG
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.docx")  # Word
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.xlsx")  # Excel
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.pptx")  # PowerPoint
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.rtf")   # RTF
gt_tbl.gtsave("my_table.typ")   # Typst
```

The image options (`zoom=`, `expand=`, and the rest) don't apply to these formats. In an Excel
workbook, each cell holds the number, date, or boolean behind its formatted text, so the values
can still be summed and sorted. SVG output is experimental in gridwell for now: it is valid and has
every cell, but its styling may change between gridwell releases.

## Choosing the Right Export Method

The following table summarizes when to use each export approach:

```{python}
import polars as pl

export_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "Method": ["show()", "as_raw_html()", "as_latex()", "gtsave()", "gtsave() with gridwell"],
    "Use Case": [
        "Interactive display in notebooks or browser",
        "Embedding in web apps, emails, or HTML docs",
        "Inclusion in LaTeX/PDF documents",
        "Static image files for reports and slides",
        "Office documents, vector graphics, and Typst",
    ],
    "Output": [
        "Rendered display",
        "HTML string",
        "LaTeX string",
        "PNG/PDF/JPEG/WebP file",
        "SVG/DOCX/XLSX/PPTX/RTF/Typst file",
    ],
})

GT(export_df)
```

Each export method preserves the styling, formatting, and structural components you have built into
your table. Choose the method that matches your final output medium, and your carefully crafted
table will look great wherever it lands.


### Extending Great Tables

The **Great Tables** package boasts a diverse range of methods for creating beautiful tables. With
no shortage of tools, styles, formats and themes, you can produce a very wide range of tables. If
you haven't yet, head over to the [examples gallery](/examples/index.qmd) for a flavor of the
variety that is possible.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="grin" arms="open up" cells="team|rating|wins|pts/Ace|4|12|88/Bolt|2|7|61" cell-trick="extend" intro='[["say", "Add-ons make me even greater!"], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

But what happens when there's something you want to add to your table, and it's not directly
supported by **Great Tables**? Let's say you have a very specific use case for your great table, so
it's not necessarily broad enough to contribute to the package. Or maybe it *is* generalizable, but
implementing it is beyond the scope of your current project. Not every feature fits neatly into a
pull request.

[**gt-extras**](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/) is a great case study in this, filling your
table desires that aren't supported by **Great Tables** directly.

This reflects a deliberate design philosophy: **Great Tables** aims to cover the most common
table-building needs out of the box, but every domain has specialized requirements. The extension
points (`fmt()`, `as_raw_html()`, `tab_style()`, and others) are intentionally designed to be
composable, so you can build domain-specific additions without forking the package. Whether you are
adding custom visualizations, specialized formatting, or entirely new layout patterns, the same
building blocks that power the built-in methods are available to you.

## Writing an Add-on Function

When adding to **Great Tables**, you have three main approaches: *wrapping*, what we might call
*composing*, and *extending*. Each takes a different angle on how to build upon the existing
functionality:

- **Wrapping** is when you simplify existing functionality by bundling common parameter
combinations. It doesn't add new capabilities, but instead makes specific or complex styling tasks
more accessible.
- **Composing** is when you combine multiple methods into a single function, allowing you to build
more complex table logic or reusable patterns.
- **Extending**, on the other hand, adds new functionality by adding behavior beyond built-in
methods. This could include processing data outside the package, or generating custom content (like
HTML or images) that gets integrated into your table.

All approaches are valuable contributions to the **Great Tables** ecosystem, and the choice between
them depends on whether you're making it easier to access existing tooling or creating entirely new
capabilities.

### Wrapping

Let's wrap `~~GT.tab_style()` to perform a specific action supported by the general function.
`~~GT.tab_style()` takes `locations=` and `style=` parameters, so let's assign those. Something this
lightweight might be useful for someone who knows what effect they want, but doesn't want to
investigate the entire space of options for styling.

```python
from great_tables import GT, loc, style


def highlight_cols(gt: GT, columns: str | list[str]) -> GT:
    locations = [
        loc.body(columns=columns),
        loc.column_labels(columns=columns),
    ]

    # Make the wrapped tab_style call
    return gt.tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="lightblue"),
        locations=locations,
    )
```

In fact, many of the functions in [**gt-extras**](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/) are
wrappers. What you see above is pulled from the source code for the function
[`gt_highlight_cols()`](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_highlight_cols), which is
a wrapper function that doesn't add *new* functionality to **Great Tables**, but instead makes a
common action much easier.

### Composing

A little more complex than wrapping, we can also compose methods to perform several steps, such as
applying multiple styles, formatting, or themes all at once.

Here's a flavor of the composed methods that **gt-extras** used in the
[ESPN theme](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_theme_espn):

```python
from great_tables import GT, google_font


def some_theme(gt: GT) -> GT:
    return (
        gt.opt_all_caps()
        .opt_table_font(
            font=google_font("Lato"),
            weight=400,
        )
        .opt_row_striping()
    )
```

This is where composing really shines. Maybe you want a very standardized look, or you want all of
your tables to mimic your favorite one. Take advantage of `~~GT.tab_options()` for your own versions
of the [premade themes](./16-premade-themes.qmd), with styles from any of the
[table theme options](./15-table-theme-options.qmd) of your choosing.

### Extending

Perhaps the most complex, this involves new behavior not supported by **Great Tables** methods
alone. Formatting values is a common way to do this:

```python
def fmt_threshold(gt: GT, columns: str | list[str], threshold: float) -> GT:
    """Format values to 0 if they are under threshold."""

    def _truncate(val: float) -> str:
        return "0" if val < threshold else str(val)

    return gt.fmt(_truncate, columns=columns)
```

Alternatively, we can extend the post-processing step by building an HTML string containing two
side-by-side tables. This function takes two separate `~~GT` objects, renders them as HTML using
`~~GT.as_raw_html()`, and then joins them in a custom HTML structure, which would not be possible
with **Great Tables** methods alone.

```python
def double_table(gt1: GT, gt2: GT) -> str:
    table_1_html = gt1.as_raw_html()
    table_2_html = gt2.as_raw_html()

    return (
        '<div style="display: flex; gap: 20px;">'
        f"<div>{table_1_html}</div><div>{table_2_html}</div>"
        "</div>"
    )
```

Again, this is a sneak peek of the **gt-extras** function,
[`gt_two_column_layout()`](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_two_column_layout),
which does a little more heavy lifting than **Great Tables** itself supports. This time, we're
adding new behavior.

## Extending with Plots

Embedded plots in tables (also known as sparklines) are a powerful tool. So much so that some
plotting is already built in, called [nanoplots](./18-nanoplots.qmd). But there are endless plot
types you could want in your great tables, and for these `~~GT.fmt()` is your friend.

When deciding between nanoplots and custom plot extensions, consider what you need. Nanoplots handle
the most common cases (line, bar, and box plots) with built-in interactivity and consistent styling
that matches your table's look. Reach for custom plot extensions when you need a chart type that
nanoplots don't support (scatter plots, pie charts, gauges, heatmap cells) or when you want full
control over the rendering using a specific plotting library's aesthetics and capabilities.

The key to adding custom plots to your tables is using `~~GT.fmt()` with a function that converts
your data values into visual representations. Your formatting function should take a value from your
table and return an HTML string containing your plot (whether that's an SVG, a series of styled
`<div>` elements, or even embedded images).

Here's a basic pattern for a plot extension:

```python
def create_my_plot(value):
    # Transform the data value into a visual representation
    # This could use any plotting library or even pure HTML/CSS
    plot_html = "<svg>...</svg>"  # Your plot generation logic here
    return plot_html


# Apply to your table
gt_tbl.fmt(fns=create_my_plot, columns="my_data_column")
```

Check out this [blog post](/blog/plots-in-tables/index.qmd) for a deeper dive into different
approaches for creating plots in tables.

## Extending with Icons

They say a picture is worth a thousand words. Maybe you want to take `~~GT.fmt_icon()` and run with
it, but with your own custom icon sets or specialized styling needs. For example:

- *Create domain-specific icon mappings:* automatically map data values to meaningful icons (like
status indicators, ratings, or categories).
- *Apply custom styling:* add animations, colors, or hover effects to your icons.

Here's an example of how you might create a custom icon extension that maps numerical ratings to
star icons:

```python
def fmt_star_rating(filled_stars: int) -> str:
    star_html = "★" * filled_stars
    return f'<span style="color: gold; font-size: 18px;">{star_html}</span>'


# Apply to your table, again `fmt()` comes in handy!
gt_tbl.fmt(fns=fmt_star_rating, columns="my_data_column")
```

## Beyond

For inspiration on ways to extend **Great Tables**, check out
[**gt-extras**](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/) and its
[source code](https://github.com/posit-dev/gt-extras).

| Function |   Type   |
|----------|----------|
| [gt_plt_bar](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_plt_bar) | Extend |
| [gt_color_box](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_color_box) | Extend |
| [gt_data_color_by_group](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_data_color_by_group) | Wrap |
| [gt_add_divider](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_add_divider) | Wrap |
| [gt_theme_538](https://posit-dev.github.io/gt-extras/reference/gt_theme_538) | Compose |


### Accessibility

Tables are read by people using screen readers and other assistive technology as well as by sighted
readers. A screen reader announces a data cell together with its headers (e.g., "Germany, GDP,
4.1"), but it can only do that when the table's structure is marked up. **Great Tables** writes that
markup into its HTML output for you, following the patterns in the W3C's
[Tables Tutorial](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/tables/). This page describes what's covered,
what isn't, and what you can do to make your tables easier for everyone to read.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="happy" arms="open rest" cells="|GDP|pop|area/Japan|4.2|124M|378k/France|3.1|68M|551k" cell-trick="read" intro='[["say", "I’ll read you any cell!"], ["mood", "grin"], ["wait", 400], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

## Row and Column Headers

Every header in a **Great Tables** table is a header cell (`<th>`) with a `scope` that says what it
labels:

- column labels and spanners are column headers (`scope="col"`, or `"colgroup"` over several
  columns)
- stub cells (the row labels) are row headers (`scope="row"`)
- an outer level of a hierarchical stub that's merged across rows, and the row group label when
  `row_group_as_column=True`, head the group of rows they span (`scope="rowgroup"`)
- row group headings and summary row labels are headers too

In tables with spanners or a hierarchical stub, `scope` alone isn't enough to tell which headers
apply to a cell, so every data cell also lists the ids of all of its headers in a `headers`
attribute. Here's a table with all of these parts:

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, data, loc, style

towny_mini = (
    data.pl.towny
    .filter(pl.col("csd_type").is_in(["city", "town"]))
    .sort("population_2021", descending=True)
    .group_by("csd_type", maintain_order=True)
    .head(3)
    .select("name", "csd_type", "population_1996", "population_2021")
)

gt_tbl = (
    GT(towny_mini, rowname_col="name", groupname_col="csd_type")
    .tab_header(title="Largest Cities and Towns in Ontario")
    .tab_spanner(label="Population", columns=["population_1996", "population_2021"])
    .cols_label(population_1996="1996", population_2021="2021")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["population_1996", "population_2021"])
)

gt_tbl
```

The first data cell's `headers` attribute refers to the row group heading, the row label, the
spanner, and the column label above it:

```{python}
import re

first_cell = re.search(r"<td headers=[^>]*>", gt_tbl.as_raw_html())
print(first_cell.group(0))
```

There's nothing to set up for any of this. Placing identifying columns in the stub with
`rowname_col=` (rather than leaving them as ordinary columns) is what makes them row headers, so do
that whenever the first column says what a row is about.

## Naming the Table

A table with a title, added with `~~GT.tab_header()`, is named after it: `<table>` refers to the
title with `aria-labelledby` (and to the subtitle with `aria-describedby`), so a screen reader
announces the title when the reader reaches the table. That's another good reason to give tables a
title, even when the surrounding text describes them.

If a page shows several tables, give each one an id with `GT(id=)`. Header ids are then prefixed by
the table's id, which keeps them unique across all of the tables on the page.

## Color and Contrast

When `~~GT.data_color()` fills cells with color, it also picks a text color (light or dark) that
contrasts with each fill, using the APCA contrast algorithm by default (`contrast_algo="wcag"`
switches to the WCAG 2 formula). Keep `autocolor_text=True` unless you're setting text colors
yourself.

Color shouldn't be the only way a table conveys meaning, since some readers can't see it or can't
tell certain colors apart. `~~GT.data_color()` keeps the values visible, so the color reinforces
them rather than replacing them. When you highlight cells with `~~GT.tab_style()`, pair the color
with another cue such as bold text, and prefer palettes that work for color-blind readers, such as
the viridis family:

```{python}
(
    gt_tbl
    .data_color(columns="population_2021", palette="cividis")
    .tab_style(
        style=style.text(weight="bold"),
        locations=loc.body(columns="population_2021", rows=pl.col("population_2021") > 500_000),
    )
)
```

## Images, Icons, Flags, and Nanoplots

Some cell contents are graphics, which screen readers can't see, so they need a text alternative:

- images from `~~GT.fmt_image()` are decorative (an empty `alt=""`) unless you give them
  alternative text with `alt=`, as a string (with `{x}` for each image's reference in the cell) or
  from a column with `~~from_column()`
- nanoplots from `~~GT.fmt_nanoplot()` are described by a summary of their values (e.g., "Line
  plot of 8 values from 12.0 to 47.0, ending at 30.0"); use `alt=` to replace or extend it (`{x}`
  is the summary)
- flags from `~~GT.fmt_flag()` are named after their country (with the default `use_title=True`)
- icons from `~~GT.fmt_icon()` are treated as decoration and hidden from assistive technology

Give images alternative text whenever they carry information, and keep a label beside any icon
that means something, since the icon itself isn't announced.

```{python}
flags_df = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "flag": ["CA", "GB", "JP"],
        "trend": ["3,5,4,8,9", "6,5,5,4,3", "2,3,3,4,6"],
    }
)

(
    GT(flags_df)
    .fmt_flag(columns="flag")
    .fmt_nanoplot(columns="trend", alt="Trend: {x}")
)
```

## Other Kinds of Output

Everything above applies to the static HTML that **Great Tables** renders in notebooks, Quarto
documents, and web pages, and to interactive tables made with `~~GT.opt_interactive()` too: the
interactivity is added to the same table markup, so its header, stub, column labels, and spanners
are kept as they are. Its controls are labeled buttons and inputs that can be used with the
keyboard, a sorted column's label says how it's sorted, and the changes readers make (sorting,
searching, filtering, or turning the page) are announced to screen readers.

LaTeX output and images saved with `~~GT.gtsave()` have no equivalent markup, so when you place a
table image in a document, describe the table in that image's alternative text or in the text
around it.

## A Short Checklist

- Put the identifying column in the stub (`rowname_col=`), and group rows with `groupname_col=`
- Give the table a title with `~~GT.tab_header()`
- Use clear column labels and spanners, since they're read aloud with every cell
- Don't rely on color alone, and keep `autocolor_text=True` with `~~GT.data_color()`
- Give tables an id (`GT(id=)`) when a page has more than one
- Give informative images alternative text (`fmt_image(alt=)`), and pair icons with a text label



## Interactive Tables

### Making Tables Interactive

**Great Tables** can make a table that readers work with in the browser: sorting it by its columns,
searching and filtering its rows, and paging through them. The table is the one you made, with all
its formatting, styles and structure; a small script that comes with its HTML adds the controls.
Nothing else is needed to view it (no server, internet connection, or other library), and the table
can be read before the script runs, or if it never does. It's interactive wherever its HTML is
shown: in Jupyter notebooks, Quarto documents, and HTML files written with
`~~GT.write_raw_html()`.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="grin" arms="rest up" cells="fruit|qty|price|kcal/fig|12|3.50|74/kiwi|40|0.80|61" cell-trick="sort" intro='[["say", "Sort me, search me!"], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

Interactive tables are ideal for exploratory contexts where the reader needs to find specific values
in a larger dataset (e.g., dashboards, internal tools, or notebook-based analysis). Sorting and
filtering let readers answer their own questions about the data without you having to anticipate
every view. For static outputs like PDF reports, printed documents, or email, stick with static
tables since the interactivity features won't be functional in those formats.

## Which one do I want?

There are two ways to make an interactive table, and they render it with the same engine.

- **`~~GT.opt_interactive()`** makes a published table browsable. It's one method, added at the
  end of a `GT` table's method chain, with options for sorting, searching, filtering, paging, and
  a few things about how the table looks. These options are the same as those of R gt's
  `opt_interactive()`.
- **`GTI`** makes the table an interface, one that readers work with. A `GTI` table is made just
  like a `GT` table, and its `i_` methods set what readers can do with it, column by column: which
  filters they get, which columns they can hide, move, or pin, how they can export the rows, how
  the table is first shown, and whether their view is kept for the next visit. A control bar below
  the table brings these together. `GTI.from_gt()` turns a `GT` table into a `GTI` one.
  [GTI Tables](26-gti-tables.qmd) is about them.

If you're publishing a table and want readers to be able to sort, search and page through it,
`opt_interactive()` is all you need. If the table is a focal point of the page (a lookup tool, a
dashboard, a view of the data that readers come back to, etc.), it's probably better to use `GTI`.

## Enabling interactivity
