A single call to `opt_interactive()` switches the table from static to interactive. The formatting
methods continue to work exactly as before.

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GT, data

gtcars_pl = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])

(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars", subtitle="The full dataset, interactively")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive()
)
```

Click the arrows under any column label to sort (or the label itself), and again to reverse the
order. Columns are sorted by their values, not by how they're formatted, so the `MSRP` column sorts
as numbers. The table is paginated by default with 10 rows per page.

You don't need to rebuild your table or learn a separate API. Instead, just append
`.opt_interactive()` to the end of your method chain. Every part of the table is kept: the header,
the stub and row groups, spanners, footnotes, source notes, and summary rows. When the rows are
sorted, they're sorted within their groups.

```{python}
gtcars_grouped = (
    data.pl.gtcars
    .filter(pl.col("ctry_origin").is_in(["Germany", "Italy"]))
    .select(["ctry_origin", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])
)

(
    GT(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="German and Italian cars")
    .tab_spanner(label="Performance", columns=["hp", "trq"])
    .cols_label(year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .opt_interactive(use_pagination=False)
)
```

## Search and filters

Pass `use_search=True` to add a search box above the table, and `use_filters=True` to give every
column a filter. Each column label then has a filter button, which opens a filter suited to the
column: a range for numbers (and dates), a list of values for a column with only a few of them,
and text to match for the rest.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Search and Filter")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, use_filters=True)
)
```

Try typing `Audi` in the search box, or setting a range in the `HP` filter, to narrow the results.

## Pagination options

Control the number of rows per page and let users choose from a list of sizes with
`page_size_default=` and `page_size_values=` (shown with `use_page_size_select=True`). The page
controls can also be changed with `pagination_type=`: `"numbers"` (a button for each page, the
default), `"simple"` (previous and next), `"full"` (first, previous, next and last, with the page
number), or `"jump"` (previous and next, with a box to type the page number in).

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Pagination options")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive(
        use_page_size_select=True,
        page_size_default=5,
        page_size_values=[5, 10, 25, 50],
        pagination_type="full",
    )
)
```

Set `use_pagination=False` to display the full table without paging. This is useful for smaller
datasets, and with `height=`, which limits the table's height and has it scroll within it, keeping
its header and column labels in view.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Scrolling")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .opt_interactive(use_pagination=False, height=400, use_compact_mode=True)
)
```

A table with thousands of rows is quicker to sort, search and filter with pagination, as only a
page of its rows is shown at a time. In Chrome and Edge, sorting a long table also takes longer if
the page it's on has CSS rules of its own that use the `:has()` selector, as these make moving
rows slower in those browsers.

An interactive table has all of its rows in its HTML, so a very large one can be slow to load,
especially on phones. You'll get a warning when a table has more than 3,000 rows or more than 10 MB
of HTML, as it's quicker to load with fewer rows (e.g., by filtering the data first) or fewer
columns. You'll also get one when a table shows more than 1,000 rows at once, all on one page or on
a page of that size, as every row shown is laid out again when the rows are sorted, searched or
filtered. To turn the warning off, use
`warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message="This interactive table may be slow")`.

A table with pagination and more than 3,000 rows has the rows past its first page in its HTML as
data, which the browser makes into rows as they're shown, so the page it's on is smaller and shows
sooner. Where the table can't run its script (e.g., in a notebook preview on GitHub), you'll see its
first page. A table written as a page with `~~GT.write_raw_html()` can have those rows in a file of
their own beside the page instead, with `GTI.i_scale(rows="asset")`: the page is smaller still,
and the browser keeps the file for later visits, but the page has to be served with the file (a
page opened from your disk can't fetch it, in most browsers).

## Styling with `tab_style()`

Styles set with `tab_style()` are part of the table's cells, so they follow the data when you sort
or filter.

```{python}
from great_tables import style, loc

(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: Targeted styles")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .tab_style(
        style=style.fill(color="#fff3cd"),
        locations=loc.body(columns="hp", rows=pl.col("hp") > 500),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.text(color="#c0392b", weight="bold")],
        locations=loc.body(columns="msrp", rows=pl.col("msrp") > 200_000),
    )
    .tab_style(
        style=[style.fill(color="#ddeeff"), style.text(weight="bold")],
        locations=loc.column_labels(columns=["hp", "trq"]),
    )
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, use_filters=True)
)
```

From the output you might notice:

- HP values over 500 are highlighted in amber
- MSRP values over \$200,000 appear in bold red
- The `HP` and `Torque` column labels have a blue-tinted background

Sort by `HP` or `MSRP` to confirm that the styling moves with the data.

## Colorizing with `data_color()`

The `data_color()` method also works in interactive tables. It applies a continuous color scale to
each cell based on the underlying value, and the colors follow the data when you sort or filter.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: data_color()")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .data_color(columns="hp", palette=["#fff7ec", "#ef6c00"])
    .data_color(columns="msrp", palette="Blues")
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True, use_filters=True)
)
```

Each column uses its own independent scale: orange for `HP` and blue for `MSRP`. The scales are
computed from the full dataset, so a cell keeps its color when you filter by `Make`. (A `GTI` table
can color them again from the rows a filter keeps instead: see
[Colors from the rows kept](26-gti-tables.qmd#colors-from-the-rows-kept).)

### Multiple columns, shared scale

Pass `domain=` to lock the color range across columns so they share a common scale.

```{python}
(
    GT(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(
        title="GT Cars: HP and Torque on a shared scale",
        subtitle="Higher values are darker and both columns use the same domain",
    )
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .data_color(
        columns=["hp", "trq"],
        palette=["#edf8fb", "#006d2c"],
        domain=[200, 1000],
    )
    .opt_interactive(use_search=True)
)
```

## Going further with `GTI`

When readers need more than `opt_interactive()` gives them, make the table a `GTI` table: its
filters, column profiles, grouping, linked tables and the explorer preset are in
[GTI Tables](26-gti-tables.qmd). Reading and setting an interactive table's view from Python (in a
notebook, in marimo, or in a Shiny, Streamlit, Panel or Solara app, which take `opt_interactive()`
tables too) is in [GTI in Python and Apps](27-gti-in-python-and-apps.qmd), as is showing tables in
pages an app makes itself, with Flask, Django or FastHTML.


### GTI Tables

When readers need more than `~~GT.opt_interactive()` gives them (see
[Making Tables Interactive](25-interactive-tables.qmd)), make the table a `GTI` table. Here, the
`Make` column gets a list of its values to choose from and `HP` a range, the table is first shown
with the most powerful cars at the top, and readers can download the rows they've filtered as CSV.

```{python}
#| include: false
# (On this page, the tables scroll sideways in a narrow container, as if made with
# `i_responsive("scroll")`, rather than being stacked as cards on a phone: the cards are shown
# once, under "Narrow containers", where they're explained)
import functools

import great_tables.gti

great_tables.gti.Settings = functools.partial(great_tables.gti.Settings, responsive="scroll")
```

```{python}
import polars as pl
from great_tables import GTI, data

gtcars_pl = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "msrp"])

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: as a GTI table")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="hp")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
    .i_export("csv")
)
```

A table you've already made with `GT()`, including one with `opt_interactive()`, becomes a `GTI`
table with `GTI.from_gt()`, keeping what `opt_interactive()` set. So does one started from a
**Polars** DataFrame's `.style` property, which makes a `GT` table, and the `i_` methods follow:

```{python}
gt_tbl = (
    gtcars_pl.style
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
)

GTI.from_gt(gt_tbl).i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
```

Each of the `i_` methods has examples on its reference page (e.g., `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()`), and
the [API Reference](/reference/index.qmd#interactive-table-controls) has them all.

## The parts of a `GTI` table

A `GTI` table is the table GT made, with a few parts added around it. Here they are in teal, on a
table that's filtered by `mfr`, sorted by `hp` and scrolls within a set height:

![A GTI table with its parts labeled. The table GT made (its column labels and body) is in gray; the parts GTI adds are in teal: the status line, column controls, column profiles, row numbers, height handle, filter tokens, and the control bar with its search, keyboard shortcuts, page controls and counter, filters as text, panels, and undo and redo.](../assets/gti_parts_of_a_table.light.svg){.lightbox width="100%"}

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="wink" arms="open" cells="Make|Model|HP|MSRP/Ferrari|F12|731|$320k/Ford|GT|647|$447k" cell-trick="export" intro='[["say", "Filter me, sort me, export me!"], ["mood", "grin"], ["wait", 400], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

From the top:

- The **status line**, just above the table, says what the data is and how much of it is shown
  ("Polars DataFrame · 12 of 47 rows × 4 columns"). It's there with `~~GTI.i_inspect()` (and in an
  explorer). In a table made with `opt_interactive(use_search=True)`, the search box is here too.
- The **column controls**, under each column label: the column's dtype (with `i_inspect()`), its
  sort arrows (with `~~GTI.i_sorting()`, on by default), and its filter button (with
  `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()`).
- The **column profiles**, under the labels of the columns `~~GTI.i_cols_profile()` chose: a small
  plot of how their values are spread.
- The **row numbers**, at the start of each row (with `i_inspect()`), which stay with the rows as
  they're sorted and filtered. A DataFrame's rows are numbered from 0, as its index is, and a
  DuckDB relation's or an Ibis table's from 1, as a database numbers them; `row_start=` in
  `i_inspect()` sets either one.
- The **height handle**, at the foot of a body that scrolls (with `~~GTI.i_scroll()`), dragged for
  a taller or shorter body.
- The **filter tokens**, one for each filter the rows are filtered by, which say what it keeps; a
  token's ✕ removes its filter.
- The **control bar**, just below the table, which brings together what readers can do with the
  table as a whole. From its left, it has:
  - the **search** (with `~~GTI.i_search()`, on by default) and the table's **keyboard
    shortcuts**
  - the **page controls**, around the **page counter** ("1 / 2"), which can be clicked to type a
    page to go to
  - the **filters as text** button (`{ }`, in a table with filters), which opens the filters as a
    query to edit, in the form `~~GTI.i_view()` takes them (with `filter=`)
  - the buttons that open the table's **panels**: its columns, grouping its rows and exporting them
    (when the table has these), and its info
  - **undo and redo** (with `~~GTI.i_view_state()`), and a **Reset** button once the view has
    changed

A table made with `opt_interactive()` has a **pager** below it instead of the control bar: its page
buttons, and the number of rows shown.

The status line and the control bar are close to the table, and the space that GT (or the page)
leaves around the table is kept past them, so that they read as part of it rather than of the text
around it.

A table names its own parts too: press `?` with the table focused (click in it first), or use
**Name the table's parts** in its info panel, and each part it has is outlined, with its name beside
it. `?` again, Escape, or a click outside the table puts the names away.

For a page that shows readers the parts, as this one does, `~~GTI.i_display()` with `parts=True`
names them from the start, and for good. Here's the table above, live: it works as ever under the
names, which follow its parts as you sort, filter, page or scroll it.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl, id="gtcars-parts")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_inspect()
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns="hp")
    .i_view(filter='mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")', sort="-hp")
    .i_view_state()
    .i_scroll(260)
    .i_display(parts=True)
)
```

## Filtering the rows

Each column given to `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()` gets a filter button under its label, which opens its
filter. The filter's type goes by the column's values, unless `type=` names one:

- `"text"` keeps the rows whose cell has what's typed, as the table shows it, ignoring case and
  accents (as the search does)
- `"facet"` is a checklist of the column's values, each with its number of rows (of those the other
  filters and the search keep); it's what a categorical column gets, and a text column with only a
  few values, each repeated
- `"range"` keeps the numbers from one to another (at least one, at most the other), for a column of
  numbers
- `"date"` keeps the dates from one to another, picked in date fields (or date and time fields, for
  a column of dates and times)
- `"bool"` keeps the rows that are true, false or missing, each with its number of rows, for a
  column of booleans

Facets, ranges, dates and booleans go by the column's values, not by how they're formatted. Here
are the half-hourly readings of May 2023 at Gibraltar's airport, with a column of dates and times
made from the dataset's text, and one saying whether there were gusts. The conditions get a text
filter (there are 22 of them, too many for a list), the times a date filter, the numbers ranges and
the gusts a bool filter. The table starts with the rainy readings from the 20th on; open the `Time`
filter to change the dates, or the `Gusts` filter for only the readings with gusts.

```{python}
weather = (
    data.pl.gibraltar.with_columns(
        when=pl.concat_str(["date", "time"], separator=" ").str.to_datetime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M"),
        gusts=pl.col("wind_gust") > 0,
    )
    .select(["when", "condition", "temp", "humidity", "wind_speed", "gusts"])
)

(
    GTI(weather)
    .tab_header(title="Gibraltar: the weather in May 2023")
    .cols_label(
        when="Time", condition="Condition", temp="Temp. (°C)", humidity="Humidity",
        wind_speed="Wind (m/s)", gusts="Gusts"
    )
    .fmt_datetime(columns="when", date_style="day_m", time_style="Hm")
    .fmt_percent(columns="humidity", decimals=0)
    .fmt_tf(columns="gusts", tf_style="yes-no")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="condition", type="text")
    .i_cols_filter(columns=["when", "temp", "humidity", "wind_speed", "gusts"])
    .i_view(filter='condition contains "rain" and when >= "2023-05-20"')
)
```

A row is shown when it passes every filter, and the search. The tokens below the table show the
filters that are on, and the `{ }` button in the control bar opens them as text, a query to edit
(with suggestions as you type), as `~~GTI.i_view()` takes it with `filter=`. Its clauses are a
column name and then:

- `contains` and a string, for a text filter (`condition contains "rain"`), or `matches` and a
  regular expression between slashes (`condition matches /^light/i`)
- `in` and values in parentheses, for a facet or a bool filter (`gusts in (true)`)
- `>=`, `<=`, `>` or `<` and a number, for a range (`temp >= 25`), or a date in double quotes, for a
  date filter (`when < "2023-05-08"`); or `top` or `bottom` and a whole number, for the rows with
  the largest or smallest values (`wind_speed top 10`)
- `is null`, for the rows missing a value, whatever the filter

The clauses are joined by `and`, and groups are written with `or`, `not` and parentheses
(`temp >= 25 or (gusts in (true) and not condition contains "fair")`); `not in`, `not contains` and
`is not null` can be written as such. A column name that isn't letters, digits and underscores goes
in backticks. A query in `i_view()` is checked against the columns' filters when the table is
shown, so a clause on a column without a filter, or with a filter of another type, is an error.

While the query is open, each filtered column's name is shown under its label, and a click on one
puts it in at the caret. Tab (or ↓) lists the columns where one can go. A column's label can be
typed in place of its name (unless another column has the same label): as its words joined by
underscores, or as it is in backticks, so a column labeled `Country of origin` can be typed as
`country_of_origin`. The name is put in its place as the word ends. The URL and `i_view()` take
only names.

## Sorting by several columns, and the keyboard

A click on a column's sort arrows (or its label) sorts the table by it: once for ascending order,
again for descending, and a third time for the table's own order. With Shift held, a click adds the
column to the sort, so that it sorts the rows the columns before it leave tied, and the arrows are
numbered in the order the columns sort the rows. Here, the cars are sorted by their make and then
from the most powerful down; Shift-click `Year` to sort the cars that tie by year as well, or click
`HP` alone to sort by it only. The info panel (from the (i) button) says how the table is sorted,
and can put it back in its own order.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: sorted by make, then horsepower")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_view(sort=["mfr", "-hp"])
)
```

`~~GTI.i_view()` takes the sort as a list of columns, the first sorting the rows and the next the
rows that tie, each with a `-` before it for descending order. Missing values are last either way.

The table's controls are buttons and fields, reached with Tab, and with the table clicked (or focus
in it) these keys work too:

- `/` opens the search, and Esc clears it, then closes it
- `←` and `→` go to the previous or next page, and Home and End to the first or last
- Shift and a click sorts by more than one column, and (with `~~GTI.i_selection()`) selects a range
  of rows
- Alt (⌥ on a Mac) with `↑` or `↓` moves a column, in the Columns panel
- Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y (⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z on a Mac) undo and redo a change to the view, with
  `~~GTI.i_view_state()`
- `?` names the table's parts

The keyboard button at the start of the control bar lists the keys the table has.

## Selecting rows

With `~~GTI.i_selection()`, readers can select rows, by clicking them or their checkboxes, in a
column before the others. With `"multiple"` (the method's default), Shift and a click selects the
rows from the last one clicked, and the checkbox in the column labels selects every row the search
and filters keep (on every page, not only the one shown); with `"single"`, selecting a row clears
the one selected before. The info panel says how many rows are selected, and its **Clear** button
clears them. Here, select a few cars, then open the export panel: with **Selected rows only**
checked, only they're exported.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: selecting rows")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_export(["csv", "clipboard"], filename="gtcars")
)
```

The selection stays as the rows are sorted, searched, filtered and paged. It's what links tables
together (see [Linked tables](#linked-tables)), and Python can read it, with the table as a widget
or in an app (see [GTI in Python and Apps](27-gti-in-python-and-apps.qmd)).

## Keeping the view

With `~~GTI.i_view_state()`, the reader's view of the table (its filters, sort, search, page, page
size, hidden columns, the column its rows are grouped by, and the height of a body that scrolls) is
kept as they change it: in the page's URL, by default, so that reloading the page, or sharing its
link, opens the table as it was; and with `storage=True`, in the browser's storage too, so that the
reader finds the table as they left it when they come back to the page. The view is kept by the
table's ID, so the table needs one (from `GTI(id=)`, or `~~GT.with_id()`). Here, choose a make or
two and sort the cars, then look at the page's address, and reload the page.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl, id="gtcars-kept")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: keeping the view")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_view_state()
)
```

In the URL, each part of the view is in the query string, named after the table's ID (as in
`?gtcars-kept.filter=mfr+in+(%22Ferrari%22)&gtcars-kept.sort=-hp`, the filter written as text),
so tables with different IDs keep their own views, and the page's other parameters are left alone.
A link with a table's view opens it with that view, rather than the one in the browser's storage. A
part of a view the table can't have (say, a filter on a column that no longer has one) is left out,
with a warning in the browser's console. The rows selected and the columns' widths aren't kept.

The control bar has undo and redo buttons (and Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y, or ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z on a Mac), and the
info panel a button that goes back to the view the table is first shown with. Undo alone,
`i_view_state(url=False)`, doesn't need an ID.

## Scrolling in place

With `~~GTI.i_scroll()`, the table takes up no more than a set height, and its body scrolls within
it. The table's header and column labels stay in view, each group's heading sticks below them while
its rows go by, and the grand summary rows at the bottom stick to the bottom. Footnotes and source
notes scroll with the body. Here are all 47 cars, with pagination off, in a body 400 pixels high.

```{python}
from great_tables import vals

gtcars_grouped = data.pl.gtcars.select(["ctry_origin", "mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq"])

(
    GTI(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: scrolling in place")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .grand_summary_rows(fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean()}, fmt=vals.fmt_integer)
    .i_pagination(False)
    .i_scroll(400)
)
```

Drag the height handle at the foot of the body down or up for a taller or shorter one, from a row's
height to all of the rows; a double click on it puts the set height back. The height can be a number
of pixels, or a CSS length such as `"60vh"`. Pagination and scrolling go together too: with both,
each page scrolls within the height.

## Wide tables

A table wider than its container scrolls sideways, with its stub (and the row group column, if row
groups are shown as one) staying in view on the left. A **Scroll for more →** hint and a shade at
the edge say there's more to the right, and the table's title, footnotes and source notes stay in
view as it scrolls. Here's every column of the cars, with each cell's text on one line (with
`~~GTI.i_display()`), which is more than this page has room for; scroll it with a trackpad, with
Shift and the mouse wheel, or by dragging the scrollbar.

```{python}
gtcars_wide = (
    GTI(data.pl.gtcars, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: every column")
    .tab_source_note("Source: the gtcars dataset.")
    .cols_label(
        mfr="Make", year="Year", trim="Trim", bdy_style="Body Style", hp="HP", hp_rpm="HP RPM",
        trq="Torque", trq_rpm="Torque RPM", mpg_c="MPG City", mpg_h="MPG Highway",
        drivetrain="Drivetrain", trsmn="Transmission", ctry_origin="Country", msrp="MSRP"
    )
    .fmt_integer(
        columns=["year", "hp", "hp_rpm", "trq", "trq_rpm", "mpg_c", "mpg_h"], use_seps=False
    )
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_display(wrap=False)
)

gtcars_wide
```

On one line, a column of text is as wide as most of its cells need, rather than as wide as its
longest: the longest tenth of them are cut short, and a cut cell shows its text in a tooltip as the
pointer rests on it (or as it's tapped). Numbers left unformatted are kept short in any interactive
table, wrapped or not: a long float, such as `0.00015800000000000002` or `1.5207923835712901e-21`, is
shown to 6 significant digits, as `0.000158` or `1.52079E-21`.

Scrolling is one of three ways `~~GTI.i_responsive()` fits a table to a narrow container; the
others, stacking the rows as cards and dropping columns, are in
[Narrow containers](#narrow-containers).

## Pinned columns

With `~~GTI.i_cols_pin()`, more columns stay in view as a wide table scrolls: pinned to the left,
after the stub, or to the right. Here's the table above, with each car's make staying by its name,
and its price at the other side.

```{python}
(
    gtcars_wide
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with pinned columns")
    .i_cols_pin(columns="mfr")
    .i_cols_pin(columns="msrp", side="right")
)
```

Pinned columns have to be next to their side of the table, with only other pinned columns between
them and it (as `mfr` is next to the stub, and `msrp` is the last column), so a column further in is
moved there first, with `~~GT.cols_move_to_start()` or `~~GT.cols_move_to_end()`. Pinned columns
can't take up more than half of the table's container; in a narrower one, only the stub stays
pinned, until the container is wide enough again. The left is the stub's side, so in a page written
right to left, the columns pinned to the "left" are on the right, by the stub.

## Narrow containers

A table wider than its container scrolls, as above, but `~~GTI.i_responsive()` has two other ways
to fit it. With `"stack"`, in a container narrower than `stack_below=` pixels (420, by default, as
on a phone), each row becomes a card, titled by its stub, with each column's label next to its
value. Row groups become headings between the cards, and summary rows cards of their own. The
column labels are shown above the cards as chips, which sort the table and open its filters as the
labels do. Here, `stack_below=` is past this page's width, so the cards are shown whatever its
width; sort by `HP` with its chip, or filter by `Make` with the filter button on its chip.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: stacked as cards")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_pagination(page_size=3)
    .i_responsive("stack", stack_below=2000)
)
```

A table is stacked by its CSS alone, so it's stacked before its script runs (or without it). The
column profiles aren't shown on the cards, and a table in a container only as wide as what's in it
(a table's cell, or an inline block) isn't stacked, unless `~~GT.tab_options()`'s
`container_width=` gives it a width of its own. That width is the one `stack_below=` is compared
with: a table with `container_width="360px"` is stacked in a wide page.

With `"collapse"`, the table drops columns until it fits: first those without a priority from
`~~GTI.i_cols_priority()` (from the last), then those with the highest numbers. A column with
priority 1 is never dropped, nor is the stub. Each row gets a button by its first cell that shows
the columns dropped from it, under it, as labels and values, and the columns come back as the
container widens. Here's the wide table of every column again, which keeps each car's make and
price, and its year and horsepower for as long as it can; it drops what this page has no room for,
and more as the window narrows. Click the arrow by a car's name to see what it dropped.

```{python}
(
    gtcars_wide
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: dropping columns to fit")
    .i_cols_priority(columns=["mfr", "msrp"])
    .i_cols_priority(columns=["year", "hp"], priority=2)
    .i_responsive("collapse")
)
```

The dropped columns are still searched, filtered and exported. They're dropped by the table's
script, so without it the table scrolls, as it does once only the columns that are never dropped are
left. By default (`"auto"`), a table drops columns if any have a priority; otherwise it's stacked
below `stack_below=` if it shows no more than six columns (not counting the stub), and scrolls if
it shows more.

## Summary rows

A `GTI` table keeps the summary rows that `~~GT.summary_rows()` and `~~GT.grand_summary_rows()` add
(see [Summary Rows](06-summary-rows.qmd)). The rows are sorted within their groups, and each
group's summary rows stay with it: those at its bottom are on the page where the group ends (and
those at its top, on the page where it starts). The grand summary rows are on every page. Here, the
most powerful cars of each country come first; page through to see each country's averages, and the
averages and highest values of all the cars under every page.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_grouped, rowname_col="model", groupname_col="ctry_origin")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with summary rows")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .summary_rows(fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean()}, fmt=vals.fmt_integer)
    .grand_summary_rows(
        fns={"Average": pl.col("hp", "trq").mean(), "Highest": pl.col("hp", "trq").max()},
        fmt=vals.fmt_integer,
    )
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_view(sort="-hp")
)
```

The summary rows' values are those found in Python, from all of the data: they don't change as
readers search or filter the rows. (Choose a make in the `Make` filter, and its country's averages
are still those of all of its cars.) A group with no rows left is hidden, with its heading and
summary rows.

## Footnotes and source notes

A table's footnotes and source notes are in its footer, as in a `GT` table, and the footnote marks
stay with their cells as the rows are sorted, filtered and paged. Here, a footnote on the `HP`
label says what it is, and another marks the cars of over 700 hp; sort by `HP` to bring them to the
top.

```{python}
from great_tables import loc

(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with footnotes and a source note")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .tab_footnote("Horsepower, at the engine's peak.", locations=loc.column_labels(columns="hp"))
    .tab_footnote("Over 700 hp.", locations=loc.body(columns="hp", rows=pl.col("hp") > 700))
    .tab_source_note("Source: the gtcars dataset.")
)
```

The marks are numbered as the table was first made, so a sorted table can have them out of order.
The search doesn't match them, and exports leave them out. A table of a lazy frame (a Polars
LazyFrame, a DuckDB relation or an Ibis table), whose rows are collected as they're shown, can have
footnotes on its title, column labels and the rest, but not on its body or stub.

## Row details

With `~~GTI.i_row_details()`, each row can have more to show under it, when the reader asks for it.
A function makes a row's details from its values (including those of columns the table hides): as
text, with `md()` or `html()`, or as a `GT` table of their own. Here, each car has a few lines about
its engine. Click the arrow by a car's name to show them, or use **Expand all** in the table's info
panel to show every car's.

```{python}
from great_tables import md


def engine(row):
    economy = (
        "" if row["mpg_c"] is None else f" It gets {row['mpg_c']:.0f} mpg in the city, "
        f"and {row['mpg_h']:.0f} on the highway."
    )
    return md(
        f"The **{row['trim']}** ({row['bdy_style']}, {row['drivetrain'].upper()}) makes "
        f"{row['hp']:.0f} hp at {row['hp_rpm']:,.0f} rpm, and {row['trq']:.0f} lb-ft of torque."
        f"{economy}"
    )


(
    GTI(data.pl.gtcars, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with row details")
    .cols_hide(
        columns=["trim", "bdy_style", "hp_rpm", "trq_rpm", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "drivetrain", "trsmn"]
    )
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", ctry_origin="Country", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_row_details(engine)
)
```

The details are in the table's HTML, made as it's rendered, but aren't searched, filtered or
exported (and each `GT` table in them brings its own CSS, so many of them make a larger page). A
column can hold them instead, with each row's details: `i_row_details()` takes its name, and the
column is then left out of the table.

## Column profiles

With `~~GTI.i_cols_profile()`, columns get a small plot under their labels of how their values are
spread: a histogram of numbers and dates, and a strip of the most common values of the others
(each value's segment as wide as its share of the rows, with its name in it if that fits), each
with the share of rows that have a missing value (and a red bar of them, last). The plots follow the rows a search or filter
keeps, so they show at a glance what's left. Here, choose a few makes in the `Make` filter and watch
the horsepower and prices narrow; point at a bar (or slide a finger along the plot) to see its
values and its number of rows. A double click or double tap on a profile (or Enter on it) opens a larger view of it, with axes, the whole caption, and each bar's rows.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: with column profiles")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_profile(columns=["mfr", "year", "hp", "msrp"])
)
```

A profile's bars span the whole column, not just the rows that are left, so that they stay put as
the reader filters (only their heights change). A strip has segments for the 5 values most rows
have, one for the other values in more than one row, and one for the values in one row each; a
column whose values are each in one row, like an ID or a name, says how many unique values the rows
have instead. Profiles aren't shown when the table is stacked as
cards in a narrow container.

## Choosing what readers can do with each column

Readers can sort, search and resize every column, by default, and hide or move none. With
`~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, each of these is set for the columns it's given:

- `sortable=False` takes away a column's sort arrows (though `~~GTI.i_view()` can still sort by it)
- `searchable=False` leaves the column's cells out of the search (though its own filter still looks
  in them)
- `resizable=False` keeps the column at its width, without a handle on its label
- `hideable=True` puts a **Columns** button in the control bar, whose panel has a checkbox for each
  of the columns, to hide it or show it again
- `reorderable=True` lists the columns in the same panel, in the order shown, where each can be
  dragged to another place, or moved with its arrow buttons (or Alt+↑ and Alt+↓)

Here, the search looks only at the cars' names and makes, the make can't be sorted by, and the
numbers can be hidden and moved: open the **Columns** panel to show the city and highway mileage,
or to put the price first.

```{python}
gtcars_cols = data.pl.gtcars.select(
    ["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "trq", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "msrp", "ctry_origin"]
)
numbers = ["year", "hp", "trq", "mpg_c", "mpg_h", "msrp"]

(
    GTI(gtcars_cols, rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: choosing the columns")
    .cols_label(
        mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", mpg_c="MPG City", mpg_h="MPG Highway",
        msrp="MSRP", ctry_origin="Country"
    )
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq", "mpg_c", "mpg_h"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_controls(columns="mfr", sortable=False)
    .i_cols_controls(columns=numbers, searchable=False, hideable=True, reorderable=True)
    .i_cols_controls(columns="ctry_origin", display=False)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="ctry_origin")
    .i_view(filter='ctry_origin in ("Italy", "Germany")', hidden=["mpg_c", "mpg_h"])
)
```

A hidden column is hidden in every row, the search doesn't look in it, and exports leave it out,
but a filter on it still keeps the rows it keeps. A column moves only among the movable columns next
to it: it can't leave its spanner, or pass a column readers can't move. The table is first shown in
the author's order, and resetting the view goes back to it.

The country of origin here is in the data but not in the table, with `display=False`: it can't be
shown, but it can be filtered by (from its token in the bar, or the `{ }` button), and the table can
be sorted by it with `i_view()`, or by a view kept in the URL. The cars start filtered to those from
Italy and Germany; remove the token to show them all. The search doesn't look in such a column and
exports leave it out, but the code copied for the view filters by it. This is also how a column that
`~~GT.cols_hide()` hid can be kept for querying.

## Colors from the rows kept

With `data_color="recompute"` in `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, a column's colors from `data_color()`
are made again from the rows a search or filter keeps, as `data_color()` would make them from those
rows alone, so that the whole palette is spread over them. Here, choose a make or two in the `Make`
filter: its most powerful car takes the darkest orange, and its most expensive the darkest blue,
however they compare to the rest of the cars. Show every row again and the first colors come back.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: colors from the rows kept")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .data_color(columns="hp", palette=["#fff7ec", "#ef6c00"])
    .data_color(columns="msrp", palette="Blues")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_cols_controls(columns=["hp", "msrp"], data_color="recompute")
)
```

Sorting the rows or turning the page doesn't change the colors. Only colors that depend on the
rows can be made again: those `data_color()` made down a column from the values it found there (not
with `domain=`, nor from an ordered categorical's levels), and without `fn=`. A cell that a later
style colors keeps that style's colors.

## Grouping rows

With `groupable=True` in `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`, readers can group the rows by any of the chosen
columns, from the **Group rows** button in the table's control bar. Each group is under a heading
with its value and its number of rows (of those a search or filter keeps), the groups in the order
of their values (or the other way around, when the column is sorted descending) with any missing
values last. The rows are sorted within their groups, and a group running over pages has its heading
on each one. Here, the cars start grouped by their country of origin, the most powerful first in
each; group them by make instead, or by none.

```{python}
by_country = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "ctry_origin", "year", "hp", "msrp"])

(
    GTI(by_country)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: grouped by country")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", ctry_origin="Country", year="Year", hp="HP", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_controls(columns=["mfr", "ctry_origin"], groupable=True)
    .i_view(sort="-hp", group_by="ctry_origin")
)
```

The column the rows are grouped by is part of the table's view, which `~~GTI.i_view()` starts the
table with (`group_by=`) and `~~GTI.i_view_state()` can keep. This grouping is the reader's: a
table with row groups of its own (from `groupname_col=`) or with summary rows can't have columns
to group by.

## Linked tables

With `~~GTI.i_link()`, tables on the same page work together: tables with the same group name are
linked by a column they each have, so that the rows a reader selects in one filter the others to the
rows with the same values. Here, select a make or two in the first table, and the second shows only
their cars; clear the selection to show them all again.

```{python}
makes = (
    gtcars_pl.group_by("mfr")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("models"), pl.col("hp").max().alias("top_hp"))
    .sort(pl.col("mfr").str.to_lowercase())
)

(
    GTI(makes, rowname_col="mfr")
    .tab_header(title="Makes")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", models="Models", top_hp="Top HP")
    .fmt_integer(columns="top_hp", use_seps=False)
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_pagination(page_size=5)
    .i_link("gtcars", on="mfr")
)
```

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]), rowname_col="model")
    .tab_header(title="Cars")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", year="Year", hp="HP", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_link("gtcars", on="mfr")
)
```

A filtered table says what it's filtered by with a token in its control bar ("Selected in Makes:
Ferrari, Lamborghini"), which goes to the selection, and whose ✕ shows every row again (until the
selection changes); its info panel says so too. The filter is on top of the table's own search and
filters, but isn't part of its view, so it isn't kept by `~~GTI.i_view_state()`. The tables link in
the browser, with no server, so this works in a Quarto document or an HTML page, and in a notebook
whose cells' outputs share a page (in Jupyter, but not in Colab, which shows each cell's output in a
frame of its own).

## How the rows look

`~~GTI.i_display()` sets how the table's rows look:

- `highlight=` (on by default) highlights the row under the pointer, or the row tapped on a touch
  screen
- `compact=True` gives the rows half of their usual padding above and below, for more of them in
  view
- `wrap=False` keeps each cell's text on one line, cut short with an ellipsis if it doesn't fit, so
  that every row is the same height
- `monospace=True` puts the column labels and the cells in a monospaced font, for a table that's a
  look at data more than a presentation of it (the title, the notes and the controls keep the
  table's font)

Here are the cars in compact rows, in a monospaced font, without the highlight:

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: compact and monospaced")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_display(highlight=False, compact=True, monospace=True)
)
```

Each call sets all of these, so `i_display(compact=True)` also puts back the highlight and the
wrapping, if an earlier call took them away. The compact rows' padding is only where the table
hasn't set its own, as with `tab_options(data_row_padding=)`.

## An explorer for looking through data

`GTI(df, preset="explorer")` starts a table set up for looking through a DataFrame rather than
presenting it:

- every column can be filtered, has a profile, and can be hidden and moved
- the rows are compact, each one line high (their text doesn't wrap), with the column labels and
  the values in a monospaced font
- the rows can be downloaded as CSV
- with `~~GTI.i_inspect()`, the rows are numbered (by their place in the data, which stays with
  them as they're sorted and filtered), each column's dtype is under its label (as Polars names it,
  whatever the DataFrame library), missing values are tinted, and the status line says what the
  data is (a Polars DataFrame or LazyFrame, a Pandas DataFrame, a PyArrow Table, a DuckDB relation,
  or an Ibis table) and how many of its rows and columns are left

```{python}
cars = data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "mpg_c", "msrp"])

GTI(cars, preset="explorer")
```

A preset is only where the table starts: the `i_` methods change it as they'd change any table. Each
sets all of its feature's settings, so `.i_display(wrap=True)` on an explorer lets its text wrap,
but also makes its rows less compact and puts them in the table's own font, unless it's given
`compact=True` and `monospace=True` too; and `.i_inspect(missing=False)` leaves the row numbers,
dtypes and dimensions on. `i_inspect()` and `~~GTI.i_display()` work on their own as well, on any
`GTI` table.

## Exporting the rows

With `~~GTI.i_export()`, an export button in the control bar opens a panel with a button for each
way readers can take the rows away: downloaded as a CSV, TSV or JSON file (`"csv"`, `"tsv"`,
`"json"`), copied (`"clipboard"`), or as code that gets them from the data (`"code"`). Here, filter
the cars to a make or two and sort them, then export what's left; the files are named
`gtcars.csv`, `gtcars.tsv` and `gtcars.json`.

```{python}
(
    GTI(gtcars_pl)
    .tab_header(title="GT Cars: exporting the rows")
    .cols_label(mfr="Make", model="Model", year="Year", hp="HP", trq="Torque", msrp="MSRP")
    .fmt_integer(columns=["year", "hp", "trq"], use_seps=False)
    .fmt_currency(columns="msrp")
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_export(["csv", "tsv", "json", "clipboard", "code"], filename="gtcars")
)
```

An export has the rows readers see: every row the search and filters keep (on every page, not only
the one shown), in the order shown, with the columns' text as the table shows it (so the Ford GT's
`MSRP` is exported as `$447,000.00`). Each format has them its own way:

- a CSV or TSV file has the column labels as its first row (each after its spanners' labels, as in
  "Revenue – gross"), and with row groups, the group's label as a column before the others; a cell
  a spreadsheet would read as a formula starts with a `'`, so that it's read as text
- a JSON file has an object for each row, with each cell's text under its column's name in the data
  (and the row's group label first, under `"group"`)
- a copy has the rows both as a table, with the cells' styles, for pasting into a document or a
  spreadsheet, and as text, with tabs between the cells
- the code filters and sorts the data (as `df`) as the reader's view does, for Polars, Pandas or
  Narwhals (the data's library, at first); it works on the data's values, so it leaves out the
  search

The formats' buttons are in the order `i_export()` is given them. With `~~GTI.i_selection()`,
readers can export the rows they've selected instead.

## Using the table from Python and in apps

Python can read what readers do with a `GTI` table and change it: in a notebook, with the table as a
widget, in a marimo notebook, and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara apps; and a page an app
makes itself, with Flask, Django or FastHTML, can show it. See
[GTI in Python and Apps](27-gti-in-python-and-apps.qmd), where a marimo notebook and a Streamlit
and a Panel app with a `GTI` table can be run in the browser, to see a selection reach Python and
Python sort the table.


### GTI in Python and Apps

An interactive table works in the browser on its own, but Python can also read what readers do with
it, and change it: in a notebook, with a `GTI` table (see [GTI Tables](26-gti-tables.qmd)) as a
widget; in a marimo notebook or app, as a UI element; and in Shiny, Streamlit, Panel and Solara
apps. These take a `GTI` table or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`, get its view and
selection, and can set them. A page an app makes itself (with Flask, Django or FastHTML) shows
the table as it works in the browser, with its runtime included once, however many tables the page
has. The notebook, marimo, Streamlit and Panel examples can each be run here, in the browser,
without installing anything; the Solara and Flask apps, which need a server, are shown as they look
when they're run.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<script src="../assets/gt-demo.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="happy" arms="point rest" cells="mfr|model|hp|mpg_c/BMW|i8|357|28/Ford|GT|647|11" cell-trick="select" intro='[["say", "Python can see what you pick!"], ["mood", "grin"], ["wait", 400], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

## Using the table from Python

In a notebook, `~~GTI.i_as_widget()` shows the table as a widget (with
[anywidget](https://anywidget.dev), installed with `pip install great_tables[widget]`), whose view
and selection Python can read and set: what the reader searched for, filtered and sorted by, the
rows that leaves, and the rows they selected. The table still works in the browser; the widget
tells Python what it shows.

```python
from great_tables import GT, GTI, data

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
widget = (
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
    .i_as_widget()
)
widget
```

With `~~GTI.i_responsive()` set to `"scroll"`, the table scrolls sideways in a narrow container (as
on a phone), rather than its rows being stacked as cards (see
[Narrow containers](26-gti-tables.qmd#narrow-containers)), as each app's table on this page does.

Then, in another cell (as the browser gives Python the table's state once the cell is done), the
cars selected, as a table of their own:

```python
chosen = widget.view(selected=True)
print(f"{len(chosen)} of {len(widget.rows)} cars selected")
GT(chosen).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
```

`widget.query` is the filters, as a query in text (e.g., `'mfr in ("Ferrari")'`), `widget.search`
the search and `widget.sort` the sort (e.g., `["-hp"]`). `widget.rows` is the data rows kept, in
the order shown (numbered from 0), and `widget.view()` gives those rows as a DataFrame of the data's
library (and `widget.view(selected=True)` the rows selected). Setting `query`, `search`, `sort` or
`selection` changes the table as shown:

```python
widget.query = 'mfr in ("Ferrari", "Lamborghini")'
widget.sort = "-hp"
widget.selection = []
```

`widget.on_change(callback)` calls `callback(widget)` after each change the reader makes. A change
made from Python is applied by the browser after the cell runs, so ask for the rows it leaves in
another cell.

Here's that notebook, run in the browser (in [JupyterLite](https://jupyterlite.readthedocs.io),
with these docs' Great Tables). Run its cells in turn, select a few cars, and then run the cells
below the table. It's also in Great Tables' repository, as
[`demos/widget/cars.ipynb`](https://github.com/posit-dev/great-tables/blob/main/demos/widget/cars.ipynb),
which can be
[opened in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/posit-dev/great-tables/blob/main/demos/widget/cars.ipynb).

```{=html}
<gt-demo src="../demos/widget/notebooks/index.html?path=_notebooks/cars.ipynb" poster="../assets/demos/widget.webp" poster-dark="../assets/demos/widget-dark.webp" height="900" label="The notebook" size="35 MB" action="Open this notebook"></gt-demo>
```

## Using the table in a marimo notebook or app

In a [marimo](https://marimo.io) notebook (or one run as an app), `mo_gti()`, from
`great_tables.marimo` (installed with `pip install great_tables[marimo]`), shows an interactive
table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) as a UI element, like marimo's own.
Assigned to a variable, the cells that read it run again with each change the reader makes. Its
`value` is a dict of the table's `"query"`, `"search"` and `"sort"`, the data `"rows"` kept (in
the order shown) and the rows in its `"selection"`. Setting the element's `query`, `search`, `sort`
or `selection` (as in a button's `on_click=`) changes the table, and the cells that read it then
run again.

```python
import marimo as mo

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.marimo import mo_gti

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = mo_gti(
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)
table
```

Then, in other cells, a button that sorts the table by horsepower, and the cars selected, as a
table of their own:

```python
def fastest(_):
    table.sort = "-hp"
    table.selection = []

fastest_button = mo.ui.button(label="Fastest first", on_click=fastest)
fastest_button
```

```python
chosen = table.view(selected=True)
mo.vstack(
    [
        mo.md(f"{len(chosen)} of {len(table.value['rows'] or [])} cars selected"),
        GT(chosen).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0),
    ]
)
```

Here's that notebook, run as an app in the browser (with marimo's WebAssembly export, and these
docs' Great Tables). Select a few cars, filter by manufacturer, or click "Fastest first":

```{=html}
<gt-demo src="../demos/marimo/" poster="../assets/demos/marimo.webp" poster-dark="../assets/demos/marimo-dark.webp" height="760" label="The marimo notebook" size="40 MB"></gt-demo>
```

`table.view()` gives the rows kept as a DataFrame of the data's library (and
`table.view(selected=True)` the rows selected). The rows are found by the browser, as the table
works there. Before the table is shown, Python finds them, except for a `GT` table with
`opt_interactive()` or a table that starts with a search: their rows are `None` until the browser
has shown the table. They're also `None` after the table's view is set (as by the button), until
the browser has applied it. Running the table's cell again makes a new table, which starts as it's
made. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) asks the notebook for each
page instead, and its rows are always found in Python.

## Using the table in a Shiny app

In a [Shiny](https://shiny.posit.co/py/) app, an interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table
with `opt_interactive()`) rendered with `render_gt()`, from `great_tables.shiny`, gives the server
its state as inputs, named after the output: `input.<id>_view()` (a dict with the `"query"`,
`"search"`, `"sort"`, `"page"`, `"page_size"`, `"hidden"` columns and `"group_by"` column),
`input.<id>_rows()` (the data rows kept, in the order shown) and `input.<id>_selection()` (the rows
selected). `update_gti()` sets its query, search, sort and selection from the server.

```python
from shiny import App, reactive, render, ui
from great_tables import GTI, data
from great_tables.shiny import output_gt, render_gt, update_gti

app_ui = ui.page_fluid(
    ui.input_action_button("fastest", "Fastest first"),
    output_gt("cars"),
    ui.output_text("chosen"),
)


def server(input, output, session):
    @render_gt
    def cars():
        return (
            GTI(data.pl.gtcars.select(["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]))
            .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
            .i_selection("multiple")
            .i_responsive("scroll")
        )

    @render.text
    def chosen():
        rows = input.cars_selection()
        return f"{len(rows)} of {len(input.cars_rows())} cars selected"

    @reactive.effect
    @reactive.event(input.fastest)
    def _():
        update_gti("cars", sort="-hp", selection=[])


app = App(app_ui, server)
```

The table works in the browser as it does anywhere else, so the server isn't asked for each page,
sort or search; a table rendered again starts with the view it's given.

## Using the table in a Streamlit app

In a [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io) app, `st_gti()`, from `great_tables.streamlit` (installed
with `pip install great_tables[streamlit]`), shows an interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT`
table with `opt_interactive()`) and gives its state: its `query`, `search` and `sort`, the data
`rows` kept (in the order shown) and the rows in its `selection`. Each change the reader makes runs
the app again, with the table's new state. `update_gti()`, called in a widget's callback, sets its
query, search, sort and selection from the app. Here, the cars selected are charted, and shown as a
table of their own (a `GT` table's HTML, with `st.html()`):

```python
import streamlit as st

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.streamlit import st_gti, update_gti

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]

st.button("Fastest first", on_click=update_gti, args=("cars",), kwargs={"sort": "-hp"})
table = (
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)
state = st_gti(table, key="cars")
st.write(f"{len(state.selection)} of {len(state.rows or [])} cars selected")

chosen = cars.iloc[state.selection]
st.bar_chart(chosen, x="model", y="hp")
st.html(GT(chosen).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0).as_raw_html())
```

Here's that app, run in the browser (with [stlite](https://github.com/whitphx/stlite), and these
docs' Great Tables):

```{=html}
<gt-demo src="../demos/streamlit/" poster="../assets/demos/streamlit.webp" poster-dark="../assets/demos/streamlit-dark.webp" height="900" label="The Streamlit app" size="45 MB"></gt-demo>
```

The table keeps its view and selection by its `key` as the app runs again, as long as it's rendered
the same. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) asks the app for each
page, which runs it again; make it once, with `st.cache_resource`, so that it isn't rendered again
each time.

## Using the table in a Panel app

In a [Panel](https://panel.holoviz.org) app or notebook, `GTIPane`, from `great_tables.panel`
(installed with `pip install great_tables[panel]`), shows an interactive table (a `GTI` table, or a
`GT` table with `opt_interactive()`) as a Panel component, whose state is in its parameters:
`query`, `search` and `sort` (a list, e.g., `["-hp"]`, which can be set to a column name, `"-hp"`,
too), the data `rows` kept (in the order shown) and the rows in its `selection`. Each change the
reader makes sets them, so that they can be used with `pn.bind()` or watched like any other
parameter; and setting `query`, `search`, `sort` or `selection` changes the table. Here, the cars
selected are shown as a table of their own, bound to the table's `rows` and `selection`:

```python
import panel as pn

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.panel import GTIPane

pn.extension()

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = GTIPane(
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)


def chosen(rows, selection):
    picked = GT(cars.iloc[selection]).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    return pn.Column(f"{len(selection)} of {len(rows or [])} cars selected", pn.pane.HTML(picked))


fastest = pn.widgets.Button(name="Fastest first")
fastest.on_click(lambda _: table.param.update(sort=["-hp"], selection=[]))
pn.Column(fastest, table, pn.bind(chosen, table.param.rows, table.param.selection)).servable()
```

Here's that app, run in the browser (converted with `panel convert`, with these docs' Great
Tables):

```{=html}
<gt-demo src="../demos/panel/" poster="../assets/demos/panel.webp" height="760" label="The Panel app" size="35 MB"></gt-demo>
```

`table.data()` gives the rows kept as a DataFrame of the data's library (and
`table.data(selected=True)` the rows selected). The `rows` are found by the browser, as the table
works there. Before the table is shown, Python finds them, except for a `GT` table with
`opt_interactive()` or a table that starts with a search: their `rows` are `None` until the browser
has shown the table. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) asks the app
for each page instead, and its `rows` are always found in Python.

## Using the table in a Solara app

In a [Solara](https://solara.dev) app or notebook, the `GTITable` component, from
`great_tables.solara` (installed with `pip install great_tables[solara]`), shows an interactive
table (a `GTI` table, or a `GT` table with `opt_interactive()`), whose `query`, `search`, `sort`
(a list, e.g., `["-hp"]`) and `selection` are the app's values, as with Solara's own components.
Each can be a reactive variable, which each change the reader makes sets and which changes the
table when the app sets it, or a value with a callback (`on_query=`, `on_sort=`, ...). One that
isn't given starts as the table has it. The data rows kept (in the order shown) are given to
`on_rows=`. Here, the cars selected are shown as a table of their own (a `GT` table's HTML, with
`solara.HTML()`):

```python
import solara

from great_tables import GT, GTI, data
from great_tables.solara import GTITable

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
table = (
    GTI(cars)
    .fmt_integer("hp")
    .fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    .i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet")
    .i_selection("multiple")
    .i_responsive("scroll")
)

sort = solara.reactive([])
selection = solara.reactive([])
rows = solara.reactive([])


def fastest():
    sort.set(["-hp"])
    selection.set([])


@solara.component
def Page():
    solara.Button("Fastest first", on_click=fastest)
    GTITable(table, sort=sort, selection=selection, on_rows=rows.set)
    solara.Text(f"{len(selection.value)} of {len(rows.value)} cars selected")

    chosen = GT(cars.iloc[selection.value]).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0)
    solara.HTML(unsafe_innerHTML=chosen.as_raw_html())
```

Saved as `app.py`, it's run with `solara run app.py` (with Great Tables, Solara and Pandas
installed), or with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), which installs them for the app:

```bash
uv run --with "great_tables[solara]" --with pandas \
  solara run app.py
```

It's also in Great Tables' repository, as
[`demos/solara/app.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/great-tables/blob/main/demos/solara/app.py).
Run, with two cars selected, it looks like this:

![The Solara app, with two cars selected](../assets/demos/solara.webp){.border fig-alt="The Solara app: a Fastest first button, the table of cars with two selected, the text '2 of 47 cars selected', and a table of the two cars."}

The component keeps the table's view as the app renders again, as long as it's given the same table
or one rendered the same. A table whose rows are kept in Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) asks the
app for each page, and its rows are found in Python; make it once (at the module's top level, as
here, or with `solara.use_memo()`), so that it isn't rendered again each time.

## Using the table in a page an app makes

An app that makes its own pages, with templates (as [Flask](https://flask.palletsprojects.com) and
[Django](https://www.djangoproject.com) apps do) or with [FastHTML](https://fastht.ml), shows an
interactive table as its HTML, which `as_raw_html()` gives: the table's `<gt-table>` element,
followed by the runtime that makes it interactive (its JavaScript and CSS). The table works in the
browser, as in an HTML file, without asking the app for anything. A table put in a Jinja template
(as Flask's are, `{{ table }}`) or in a FastHTML component (`Div(table)`), or returned by a
FastHTML route on its own, is shown as its HTML, as it is.

A page with several tables needs the runtime only once: `runtime_tags()`, from
`great_tables.web`, gives it, for the page's `<head>`, and each table is then given without it,
with `as_raw_html(runtime="none")`. With `url=`, the tags link to the runtime's files, which
`write_runtime()` writes for the app to serve, so that a browser keeps them as it does any other
file. Here, they're written to the folder Flask serves as `/static/` (`app.static_folder`, beside
the app, wherever it's run from):

```python
from flask import Flask, render_template_string
from markupsafe import Markup

from great_tables import GTI, data
from great_tables.web import runtime_tags, write_runtime

cars = data.gtcars[["mfr", "model", "year", "hp", "msrp"]]
app = Flask(__name__)
write_runtime(f"{app.static_folder}/gti")

PAGE = """
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>{{ runtime }}</head>
<body>{% for table in tables %}{{ table }}{% endfor %}</body>
</html>
"""


@app.route("/")
def index():
    table = GTI(cars).fmt_integer("hp").fmt_currency("msrp", decimals=0).i_responsive("scroll")
    tables = [table.i_cols_filter(columns="mfr", type="facet"), table.i_selection("multiple")]
    return render_template_string(
        PAGE,
        runtime=runtime_tags(url="/static/gti/"),
        tables=[Markup(table.as_raw_html(runtime="none")) for table in tables],
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run()
```

Saved as `app.py`, it's run with `python app.py` (or `flask --app app.py run`, with Great Tables,
Flask and Pandas installed), or with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/):

```bash
uv run --with great_tables --with flask --with pandas app.py
```

It's also in Great Tables' repository, as
[`demos/flask/app.py`](https://github.com/posit-dev/great-tables/blob/main/demos/flask/app.py).
Its page, with two cars selected in the second table, looks like this:

![The Flask app's page, with two cars selected in its second table](../assets/demos/flask.webp){.border fig-alt="The Flask app's page: a table of cars with a facet filter by manufacturer, and below it the same table with checkboxes, two of them checked."}

Django makes what's put in a template a string before it's shown, so a table is given as its HTML,
marked safe (with `mark_safe(table.as_raw_html())`, or `{{ table_html|safe }}` in the template);
the runtime's tags are shown as they are. In FastHTML, the HTML of a table without its runtime is
given as `NotStr(table.as_raw_html(runtime="none"))`, and the tags as one of the app's headers
(`fast_app(hdrs=(runtime_tags(),))`).

A page whose Content Security Policy allows no inline scripts can have the runtime from its files
(`script-src 'self'`), or inline with the policy's nonce (`runtime_tags(nonce=...)`); the table's
spec, in a `<script type="application/json">`, is data, which isn't run. The table's own CSS is
inline, so the policy's `style-src` must allow `'unsafe-inline'`. A table whose rows are kept in
Python (with `~~GTI.i_scale()`) needs an app that answers its asks for pages, so in a page an app
makes, its rows are in the browser.



## Reference

### Glossary

Terms used throughout the **Great Tables** documentation, listed alphabetically. Where a term
has a direct counterpart in the API, the relevant class, method, or module is noted.

```{=html}
<script src="../assets/tabblen.js" defer></script>
<gt-tabblen float="right" mood="thinking" arms="rest" cells="A–F|G–L|M–S|T–Z/Body|Header|Stub|Title/Footer|Locale|Style|" cell-trick="define" intro='[["say", "All the table words, A to Z!"], ["mood", "happy"]]'></gt-tabblen>
```

Body
: The main data area of the table, consisting of rows and columns of cells that hold the
  underlying data values (after any formatting or substitution has been applied). The body
  excludes the **header**, **column header**, **stub**, **footer**, and any **summary rows**.
  Targetable with `loc.body()`.

Cell
: A single value at the intersection of a row and a column within the **body**, **stub**, or
  **summary rows**. Cells are the fundamental unit that **formatters**, **styles**, and
  **footnotes** act upon.

Column controls
: In a **GTI table**, the small controls under each **column label**: the column's dtype (with
  `~~GTI.i_inspect()`), its sort arrows (with `~~GTI.i_sorting()`, on by default), and its
  **filter** button (with `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()`). What readers can do with each column (sort,
  search, resize, hide, move or group by it) is set with `~~GTI.i_cols_controls()`.

Column header
: The region directly above the **body** that contains all **column labels** and any
  **spanner labels**. It provides the labeling structure that maps data columns to their
  display names and groupings. Targetable as a whole with `loc.column_header()`.

Column labels
: The individual text labels that identify each column in the table. By default they are the
  column names from the input DataFrame, but they can be overridden with `cols_label()` or
  transformed with `cols_label_with()`. Targetable with `loc.column_labels()`.

Column profile
: In a **GTI table**, a small plot under a **column label** showing how the column's values are
  spread: a histogram for numbers and dates, and a strip of the most common values of other
  columns, with the share of missing values. Profiles follow the rows the **search** and
  **filters** keep. Added with `~~GTI.i_cols_profile()`.

Column selector
: An expression passed to a `columns=` parameter to identify which columns an operation
  should act on. Accepts a column name (string), a list of names, an integer index, a Polars
  selector expression (e.g., `cs.numeric()`), or a callable that takes a column name and
  returns a boolean. Column selectors are used throughout the API in methods like
  `~~GT.fmt_number()`, `cols_align()`, `tab_style()`, and many others.

Control bar
: The row of controls just below a **GTI table** that brings together what readers can do with
  the table as a whole: the **search** and keyboard shortcuts, the **page controls**, the
  **query** button (`{ }`), the buttons that open the table's **panels**, undo and redo (see
  **view state**), and a Reset button once the **view** has changed. A table made with
  `opt_interactive()` has a **pager** instead.

Data color
: A technique for colorizing **cell** backgrounds based on data values, providing a visual
  encoding of magnitude or category directly in the table. Applied with `data_color()`, which
  supports custom palettes, ColorBrewer palettes, domain specification, and automatic
  contrasting text color.

Filter
: In an **interactive table**, a control that keeps only the rows matching a condition on one
  column, opened from the column's filter button. A **GTI table** gets filters with
  `~~GTI.i_cols_filter()`, of five types: `"text"`, `"facet"` (a checklist of values), `"range"`,
  `"date"`, and `"bool"`. A row is shown when it passes every filter and the **search**.

Filter tokens
: In a **GTI table**, a token for each **filter** in use, shown below the table, that says
  which rows the filter keeps. A token's ✕ removes its filter.

Footer
: The bottom region of the table, below the **body** and any **summary rows**. It contains
  **footnotes** and **source notes**. Targetable as a whole with `loc.footer()`.

Footnote
: An annotation consisting of two linked parts: a **footnote mark** placed at a specific
  location in the table, and the corresponding footnote text rendered in the **footer**. Added
  with `tab_footnote()`. When multiple footnotes share the same text, the mark is reused
  rather than duplicated.

Footnote mark
: A small symbol (number, letter, or typographic symbol) attached to a **cell** or label in
  the table that links it to its corresponding **footnote** text in the **footer**. Marks are
  ordered left-to-right, top-to-bottom according to their position in the table. The mark
  style is configured with `opt_footnote_marks()`, which accepts keywords like `"numbers"`
  (the default), `"letters"`, `"LETTERS"`, `"standard"` (four traditional symbols), or
  `"extended"` (six symbols), as well as custom lists of strings.

Formatter
: A method that transforms how raw data values are displayed in **cells** without altering the
  underlying data. All built-in formatters follow the `fmt_*()` naming convention (e.g.,
  `~~GT.fmt_number()`, `~~GT.fmt_currency()`, `~~GT.fmt_date()`). A general-purpose `fmt()` method
  accepts a custom formatting function. The `vals` module provides standalone equivalents for use
  outside a `GT` object, such as in **summary rows** definitions.

Grand summary rows
: Aggregation rows that summarize the entire table's data, regardless of **row groups**.
  Created with `grand_summary_rows()` and placed at the very bottom of the **body** (above the
  **footer**). Targetable with `loc.grand_summary()`.

GT object
: The central object in **Great Tables**, created by passing a Polars, Pandas, or PyArrow table
  to `GT()`. All table-building operations are methods on this object and return a modified copy,
  enabling method chaining. Optional constructor arguments include `rowname_col` (to create a
  **stub**), `groupname_col` (to create **row groups**), `locale`, and `id`.

GTI table
: An **interactive table** made with `GTI()` rather than `GT()`, built like a **GT object** and
  rendered as a table readers work with. Its `i_` methods set what readers can do with it, column
  by column: which **filters** they get, which columns they can hide, move or pin, how they can
  export the rows, and how the table is first shown (its **view**). `GTI.from_gt()` turns a `GT`
  table into a `GTI` table.

Header
: The topmost region of the table, positioned above the **column header**. It contains the
  **title** and optionally a **subtitle**. Set with `tab_header()`. Targetable as a whole with
  `loc.header()`.

Height handle
: In a **GTI table** whose body scrolls within a set height (with `~~GTI.i_scroll()`), the handle
  at the foot of the body that readers drag for a taller or shorter body. A double click on it
  restores the set height.

Hidden column
: A column that is present in the underlying data but not rendered in the output table.
  Columns can be hidden with `cols_hide()` and restored with `cols_unhide()`. Hidden columns
  remain accessible for operations like **merged columns** patterns, **data color** mapping,
  and `from_column()` references.

Interactive table
: A table that readers can sort, search, filter, and page through in the browser, with no server
  or other library needed. It's made either by adding `opt_interactive()` to a `GT` table's method
  chain, for a published table that readers can browse, or as a **GTI table**, for a table that is
  an interface. Both keep the table's formatting, styles, and structure.

Linked tables
: **GTI tables** on the same page that work together through `~~GTI.i_link()`: the rows a reader
  selects in one (see **selection**) filter the others to the rows with the same values in a
  shared column.

Locale
: A language/region identifier (e.g., `"en"`, `"de"`, `"fr-CA"`) that controls how **formatters**
  render numbers, currencies, dates, and times. Locale determines things like the decimal mark,
  digit grouping separator, currency symbol, and date/time patterns. Set at the table level with
  `GT(locale=...)` or `with_locale()`, or overridden per formatter call.

Location selector
: An object from the `loc` module that identifies a specific region or set of **cells** in
  the table. Location selectors are used in `tab_style()` to target where styles are applied
  and in `tab_footnote()` to place **footnote marks**. Examples include `loc.body()`,
  `loc.column_labels()`, `loc.stub()`, and `loc.header()`.

Merged columns
: A display technique that combines content from multiple columns into a single column using
  a pattern string. Created with `cols_merge()`, where the pattern uses `{0}`, `{1}`, etc. to
  reference column values (e.g., `"{0} ({1})"`). Conditional removal of content when values
  are missing is supported via `<<`/`>>` delimiters in the pattern. Convenience variants
  include `cols_merge_uncert()`, `cols_merge_range()`, and `cols_merge_n_pct()`.

Nanoplot
: A tiny inline visualization embedded directly in a table **cell** via `fmt_nanoplot()`.
  Supports `"line"`, `"bar"`, and `"boxplot"` plot types, with optional reference lines,
  reference areas, and automatic y-axis scaling across rows. Appearance is customized through
  `nanoplot_options()`.

Page controls
: In a **GTI table**'s **control bar**, the buttons for the first, previous, next, and last pages,
  around the page counter ("1 / 2"), which can be clicked to type the page to go to. The page
  size is set with `~~GTI.i_pagination()`.

Pager
